## THE WORKMANSHIP OF THE WORLD
->THAT IS<-

The nature, powers, properties, and the composition and structure of each part of the celestial expanse and the stars—both wandering <note>the planets</note> and fixed—from the lowest globe of the Earth all the way to the final boundaries of the World, explored through the veil of a fictional rapture <note>or visionary journey</note>, is set forth according to truth by a new hypothesis.

->Queen of the Swedes, Goths, and Vandals<- <note>Christina (1626–1689) was a formidable intellectual and patron of the arts. She abdicated the Swedish throne in 1654, converted to Catholicism, and moved to Rome, where she became a central figure in the city's scientific and cultural life.</note>

->*ATHANASIVS KIRCHERVS*<-
->*of the Society of JESUS.*<- <note>The Society of Jesus, or the Jesuits, was the Catholic religious order to which Kircher belonged. They were renowned for their rigorous scientific education and missionary work.</note>

**H**EAVEN I unfold to you, wise Queen; Heaven, I say, like a book folded into various arrangements of the stars, distributed into just as many chapters, as if by a division of multifaceted reasoning; whose characters <note>Kircher is using the metaphor of the "Book of Nature," a common 17th-century idea that God's creation could be "read" like a second Bible through science and observation.</note>

He sets out this book for you to read: by day, as if on the whitest pages of a countless variety of things; by night, indeed on black pages, yet inscribed with golden letters—that is, wonderfully visible in the radiant cloak of the stars. *Man is the index and summary of the book*; the censor and approver was He who saw that all things which He had made were very good <note>A reference to the biblical account of Creation in Genesis, where God "saw that it was good."</note>.

...was raging with lightning and echoing with thunder; here, beyond the eclipses <note>original: "labores"; literally "labors," a term used in Latin to describe the perceived struggle or toil of the sun and moon during an eclipse.</note> of the Moon and the Sun, individual stars revolved in their own motions; here night followed day and day followed night in alternating succession; while the King alone triumphed unharmed in the very center, as if on the central throne of the world. 

You, O Queen, not unlike this, shall occupy the center of Heaven, immune and free from all injuries of the weather <note>original: "meteororum"; in the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including storms, rain, and wind.</note>, destined to be the center and heart of the planets and stars. Your genius, your celestial nature, and the eminence of your mind—eager for every <term>encyclopedia</term> <note>original: "encyclopedię"; from the Greek for the "circle of learning," referring here to the mastery of all sciences and arts.</note>—has destined you for this wise place in Heaven. 

Travel now for a little while in this Heaven, so that you may eventually rest, not as a stranger but in your true homeland, in that genuine Kingdom of the Heavens. To seek that Kingdom, you voluntarily departed as a pilgrim from your own Kingdom and Fatherland, surpassing the glory of a worldly crown <note>This refers to Queen Christina’s famous abdication of the Swedish throne in 1654 and her subsequent journey to Rome.</note>; you have shown how much you value that Kingdom—the Kingdom of all ages.

Enter, O Queen, this heaven of mine; enter with Wisdom as your companion, *which alone circled the vault of Heaven* <note>A reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 24:5, where Wisdom describes her own divine authority over the cosmos.</note>, since from this Heaven...

as if by a manifold arrangement of steps, you will ascend to the Author of Heaven himself, as if to the throne of the eternal Solomon <note>King Solomon was legendary for his wisdom; here, Kircher compares the Queen’s pursuit of knowledge to an approach toward divine wisdom.</note>; there you will look more deeply into what that golden eternity of immortal treasures in the Kingdom of GOD might be—that eternity which you, as a true <term>Urania</term> <note>original: "Vrania"; the Muse of Astronomy in Greek mythology, used here to represent the Queen as a scholar of the stars.</note> and watcher of the Heavens, have sought with this more-than-Royal majesty of your exalted soul, and by such an unexpected example of Royal conduct <note>A reference to her abdication and conversion to Catholicism, which shocked the European political world.</note>. You will find among the works which GOD, the Author of all things, brought forth in the beginning, that the first book was the Heaven; I pray to GOD from the very marrow of my soul <note>original: "omnibus animi medullis"; a Latin idiom meaning "with the utmost sincerity" or "from the bottom of my heart."</note> that, having unrolled this book through constant contemplation of the mind, you may finally attain the acquisition of its incorruptible goods. Farewell, and may you long remain safe for the sake of the Christian Commonwealth.

# GOSWIN NICKEL
## Superior of the Society of JESUS
### General.

**S**INCE several theologians of our same Society have reviewed the small work titled the **Ecstatic Journey** <note>original: "Itinerarium exstaticum"; this is Kircher’s famous work on astronomy and cosmology, presented as a visionary journey through the heavens.</note>, by **Father Athanasius Kircher**, a Priest of our Society, and have approved that it may be brought into the light <note>original: "in lucem edi"; a standard Latin idiom meaning "to be published."</note>, we grant permission for it to be sent to the press, if it shall so seem fit to those to whom it pertains. In witness of which, we give these letters signed by our hand and secured with our seal at Rome, **November 15, 1655.**

*Goswin Nickel.*

---

*I*T IS SO, Reader; so sweetly does the eternal wisdom of God play upon the Earth, that scarcely has an age existed so crude and unpolished that He has not gladdened the World—as if it were nauseated by <note>original: "nauseabundum"; suggests the world is weary or "sick" of the same old things</note> old things—with new spectacles of His divine power, and instructed it with new preludes of the great stage <note>A reference to the "theatrum mundi" or "world stage," a common 17th-century metaphor where the universe is a theater directed by God.</note>; so that by this very means He might seize men into love and admiration of Himself; and if ever they should turn aside from the path of divine commandments, [He might recall them] by the fearsome [monitions] of por-<note>The text breaks here; the catchword "stris" on the bottom of the page indicates the full word is "monstris" (portents or omens).</note>

# ->Preface<-

*tents, God might lead transgressors back to the heart. Just as it happened in times past, so too in these most recent centuries it has occurred to the great astonishment of mortals. Venerable antiquity knew nothing of the existence of a New World <note>original: "noui Orbis"; referring to the Americas</note> in the nature of things, nothing of the vast spread of the Ocean around the globe, and nothing of the state of the Antipodeans <term>Antichtones: inhabitants of the opposite side of the Earth, whose existence was a subject of intense debate among ancient and medieval scholars</term>; when behold, God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Deus Opt: Max:" (Deus Optimus Maximus), a title for God adapted from the Roman title for Jupiter</note>, after the times of His inscrutable counsel were fulfilled, opened to us a new theater of the World <note>original: "Mundi theatrum"</note>, filled with such a variety of exotic things as we read with wonder in the records of the historians of the New World. If anyone had related these things to the Ancients, they would undoubtedly have judged them not as plausible histories, but as pure fables and the ravings of old women <note>original: "anilia deliramenta"</note>. The play of divine kindness did not stop here; for within a not-so-long interval of years after the discovery of the New World, He unfolded for us a new theater of celestial spectacles, and revealed things unheard of in all past ages through the benefit of the celestial tube <term>Celestial tube: "coelesti tubi," an early 17th-century term for the telescope</term>. The construction of the world machine <term>World machine: "Mundanæ machinæ," a common metaphor for the universe as a complex, divinely-engineered mechanical system</term> had, from time immemorial until now, shown men only the external beauty of its face; but now, having peeled back the bark, He has uncovered the kernel. With the barriers opened, He has revealed the internal state of things: the position of the gears <note>original: "rotarum," literally "wheels," referring to the mechanics of planetary orbits</note>, the arrangement and proportion of the spheres, the composition of the globes, the duties of the centers, and the matter and form by which individual parts are com-* <meta>The text ends mid-sentence; the final word "compo-" likely completes as "componuntur" (are composed) on the next page.</meta>

# ->To the Reader<-

*...set forth, [it] shows; it lays open the hidden paths of motions, and has explained the nests of light and heat with such amazement from the Philosophers <note>In the 17th century, "Philosophers" usually referred to natural scientists</note>, that there was almost no one who did not rush with armed eyes <term>Armed eyes: "armatis oculis," a common 17th-century metaphor for eyes aided by optical instruments like telescopes</term> to contemplate the unusual portents of nature with the greatest effort. Here, onto the stage of heaven, have come forth—beyond the ancient ones, which were formerly indistinct in the nebulous stars—throngs of numerous stars throughout the whole circuit of the Galaxy <note>The Milky Way</note>; as well as the births of new stars in Cassiopeia, Ophiuchus <note>original: "Serpentario," the Serpent-Bearer constellation</note>, and Cygnus, differing in a wonderful manner in their nature, properties, shape, and diversity of colors; to say nothing, for now, of the variety of Comets, those dire omens for mortals. Here the Sun—than which the world has until now believed nothing to be clearer or more shining—appeared transformed by a certain wonderful variety of spots <term>Sunspots: "macularum," the dark patches on the Sun observed by early telescopists</term> and shadows; and, as if struggling with huge surgings of tides <term>Ebullitions: "ebullitiones," bubbling or boiling up; here describing the turbulent solar surface</term>, that most constant star of the World appeared subject to a perpetual succession of changes. Here the Moon presented herself on the stage, laden with mountains, lakes, seas, and islands; followed by Venus, who showed herself with a horned brow <note>original: "corniculata fronte," referring to the discovery that Venus has phases like the Moon</note> and, due to the roughness of her parts, not nearly so beautiful as the Ancients believed. Mercury, bright yet rough and divided into various phases, offered a wonderful sight; then Mars, fierce with a certain hunchbacked and blunt, not quite round shield <note>original: "umbone," referring to the appearance of the planet's disk</note>, and grim with a rust-colored spot and formidable with the belching of fire; then*

# ->Preface<-

*The star of Jupiter is surrounded by fourfold splendors, not so much satellites as "Little Kings"* <note>original: "Regulorum." This refers to the four "Medicean Stars" discovered by Galileo—the moons Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto.</note>; *it is encircled crosswise by a* 
<margin>belt</margin> 
*belt, rarely a single one, more often a double one, and even more rarely a triple one* <note>These "belts" are the atmospheric cloud bands of Jupiter.</note>. *Finally, Saturn closes the ranks of the planets; like a Geryon* <note>Geryon was a giant in Greek mythology with three bodies; early telescopes were not powerful enough to resolve Saturn's rings, making the planet appear as three separate parts.</note>, *it showed itself in a form awesome to behold, a monster and marvel of a three-bodied star.*

*And so, although this new apparatus of the World and the unheard-of fertility of playful Nature drew the eyes of all Astronomers to itself, it can hardly be said how much the causes of such unusual effects tortured the intellect of everyone. And just as rumors of unusual things prick the ears of all in a wonderful way, so too did they anxiously stimulate the curiosity not only of Mathematicians and Philosophers* <note>In this era, "Philosophers" referred to natural scientists.</note>, *but even of Princes. Among these may be rightly numbered the most August Emperor Ferdinand III* <note>Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1637–1657) and a significant patron of the arts and sciences.</note>, *a most munificent Patron. ## AN ENCOURAGING INTRODUCTION,

*In which the Author clearly teaches that this little work contains nothing foreign that does not*
->*agree*<-
*with the authority of Holy Scripture and the Holy Doctors of the Church, as well as the unassailable experiments of observation,*

As I prepare to set forth this *Ecstatic Journey* <term>Itinerarium exstaticum: a spiritual and intellectual voyage through the cosmos, framed as a vision or dream</term>, I have decided to first reveal my mind to the curious Reader regarding several matters that are absolutely necessary to know. In this way, the Reader may traverse the path through the heavenly regions—which we are about to open—with the hoped-for benefit, and walk through the hidden paths of higher nature with an unhindered foot. I confess that many things occur within it which might not undeservedly seem entirely new, paradoxical, and unheard of until now to someone inexperienced in the study of nature. # EXHORTATIONS

[...so that it] agrees. In order that this may be demonstrated, four points must be proven by me in this *Journey* <term>Itinerarium: the author's term for this intellectual and spiritual voyage</term>. If these points are judged—as I hope—correctly, sincerely, and free from all deceit and the disturbance of biased emotion, I certainly trust that I shall obtain full faith in the truth that shines forth in the craftsmanship of the world <note>original: "mundi opificio"</note> and the structure of the heavenly bodies.

**First** is that in the Celestial World, if you except the bodies of the stars themselves, no other solidity can or should be admitted; and thus the entire heaven, from the highest region of the air all the way to the Empyrean heaven <term>cœlum empyreum: in medieval and Renaissance cosmology, the highest, most refined part of the heavens, often considered the dwelling place of God</term>, is liquid and ethereal.

**Second** is that there is no body in the nature of things which is not subject to alterations and corruptions in some part; and thus all the globular bodies of the stars are subject to these laws of alteration by a certain necessity of nature—as they could not exist without them—and therefore the heaven, along with all its universal bodies, is corruptible <note>The author is challenging the ancient Aristotelian view that the heavens were "incorruptible" and unchanging, a major shift in 17th-century science</note>.

**Third**, that all the starry bodies of the World are composed of a mixture of the four elements <term>quatuor elementorum mixtura: the classical elements of Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</term> in a manner suitable to them, no differently than the Earth, though endowed with different properties and qualities; just as each was equipped with its own specific centers by the Supreme Architect of the World.

**Fourth**, according to a certain analogy, all the bodies of the World stand in the same relation to one another as the Sun, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, and the Earth stand to one another. 

Indeed, I could prove these things at length in this place with cited authorities, were it not that distinguished men have already done so in entire volumes—namely, Father Giovanni Battista Riccioli in the *New Almagest* <note>original: "Almageſto nouo" — an encyclopedic work of astronomy published in 1651 by the Jesuit astronomer Riccioli</note>, and Father Christopher...

# Prelude

...[by all these] factors, driven both by Princes of the highest authority and by my own curiosity for investigating the secrets of nature, it seemed fit to compose this present little work. In it, I retain the substance of everything explained by the Holy Fathers and established by modern observations; however, I proceed with a different method, resolving each point to its ultimate principles in a way that, as far as I know, perhaps no one has done before me. I have done this to such an extent that whatever I have brought forward in this entire little work regarding the wonders of marvelous <term>phenomena</term> <note>Original Greek: φαινομένων (phainomenon), meaning "appearances" or things observed in the sky.</note> may be called not so much inventions fashioned by my own wit, but rather certain logical consequences resulting from the stated authorities and observations. 

I have used this reasoning: if the heaven, or firmament, is liquid <note>In this context, "liquid" (liquidum) means fluid or flowing, like air or water, rather than a solid crystalline sphere as older medieval science suggested.</note>, as the Holy Fathers explain from Sacred Scripture, then the heaven must be one and threefold, everywhere passable and everywhere penetrable, placing no obstacles or barriers to the astral bodies <note>The stars and planets.</note> moving within it. It is one in its continuous fluidity, yet threefold in the distinction of its regions; these are the aerial, the starry, and the empyrean heaven. It is to this last one that they say Saint Paul was caught up; yet, just as it is far removed beyond all limits of the natural order, it is reached by faith alone.

He explains this more at length in chapters 7, 9, and 10, where he does nothing else than provide a rigorous [explanation] to those consulting him about these sayings...

# Exhortations.

...[one should] dissuade against the hardness of the firmament; <margin>St. Basil.</margin> Saint Basil, another light of the Church, along with countless other Fathers cited by the aforementioned authors, completely mocks the idea of the solidity of the heavens and openly declares it to be a childish invention. *Indeed, in the cited homily <note>Original: "hom. cit." referring to Basil's Homilies on the Hexaemeron, or the Six Days of Creation.</note>, he argues in this way: "Yet the firmament itself, although according to common and popular understanding it seems to have had its origin from water, should by no means be considered similar either to water hardened into ice or to any such material which takes the beginning of its origin from strained moisture, such as the nature of crystal stone is known to be." <note>In antiquity and the Middle Ages, rock crystal was often thought to be water that had frozen so intensely it could never melt.</note> And a little later: "Therefore, we judge the firmament to be like none of these; for it is truly the mark of a childish and simple mind to hold such opinions about the celestial bodies. Nor yet—since all things are in all, fire in air, air in water, and of the others one is in another, and absolutely none of those elements which fall under our senses is pure or lacks a mixture, so as not to share in a middle or opposite state—does it please us to assert that the firmament is for that very reason either from one of the elements or mixed from all of them, we who have now been so instructed by Divine Scripture, etc."*

<margin>The words of St. Basil in the Hexaemeron <note>A Greek term meaning "Six Days," referring to the biblical account of Creation.</note> concerning the firmament.</margin> *Since these things are so, once you have rejected that foolish wisdom (of the Philosophers) who deny and mock the "waters above the heavens" <note>A reference to Genesis 1:7. It may be unrefined in speech, but it is stable and firm in knowledge, concerning what the name "firmament" signifies in Scripture. It certainly suggests a nature that is by no means resistant or solid, or something heavy with its own weight or unyielding. He says the firmament is not of that kind; otherwise, if you understand its mass to be heavy in that way, na-* <note>The text cuts off mid-word; the catchword "tu-" on the previous page indicates the word is "natura" (nature).</note>

Certainly, I find no other cause for this phenomenon except this: that the solar rays were intercepted by the vapors surrounding the Moon, from which a greater light seems to arise in place of **Solar spots** and **Comets**. # Exhortatory Reflections

<meta>Catchword: in</meta>

...terrestrial matter, from which the globes are formed, necessarily behaves no differently than on Earth, where heat acting upon moisture dissolves it; the moisture inherent in bodies, thinned by heat, passes into a subtle substance which astronomers call an **atmosphere**; whether that globe is composed of liquid fire or fluid water. For as **Saint Ambrose** <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397 AD), the Bishop of Milan and a highly influential theologian who wrote on the creation of the world.</note> rightly says in Book 1, Chapter 6 of his *Six Days of Creation* <note>original: "Hexam:" or *Hexameron*, a series of homilies on the biblical creation story.</note>: *It is enough,* he says, *for the present assertion, that in the beginning He made heaven, from which the cause of generation <note>The process of coming into being or being born.</note> comes, and earth, in which the substance of generation resides; for in these the elements were created, from which all those things which belong to the World are generated: the four elements, moreover, are **Air**, **Fire**, **Water**, and **Earth**, which are mixed with one another in all things.* 

From these words, it is clearly evident that in all the globes of the World—as they do not differ in kind from sublunary <note>Meaning "below the moon," referring to the Earthly realm which was thought to be subject to change, unlike the "unchanging" heavens.</note> elementary matter—they are likewise subject to the laws of **generation and corruption** <note>A standard philosophical term of the era meaning "birth and decay."</note>. In each of these globes, heavy things tend toward the center of each body, while light things, exhaled from the center through the dissolving of moisture by heat, produce that outflow which astronomers call the **atmosphere**. 

For since sensory experience has found all the bodies of the World to be opaque, it is certain that the rays of the **Solar** bodies, striking them—surfaces which are wonderfully roughened by the inequality of their parts—intensify the heat to the highest degree, just as happens on Earth from the reflection of Solar light. From this intensification of heat, a **resolution** <note>The process of a solid or liquid substance turning into vapor.</note> of the moisture existing within the terrestrial substance occurs; from resolution comes **rarefaction** <note>The process of becoming less dense.</note>; from rarefaction, at the more remote boundary of the **atmosphere**, a **condensation** occurs again due to the breath of the neighboring cold **ether** <note>The "ether" was believed to be the fluid that filled the void of space beyond planetary atmospheres.</note>; and finally from condensation...

Therefore, no one should wonder if we assert that the celestial globes of a solar nature are composed of liquid fire and an earthy portion, while those of a lunar nature are composed of water and an earthy substance; for these conclusions are drawn by natural consequence from our previous assumptions. For whatever must be thought to happen on the terrestrial globe, we should likewise suppose happens in celestial bodies according to a certain analogy. Thus, it can certainly be inferred that whatever actions follow the joining of elements are found in celestial globes—more in one, and less in another. 

Therefore, in addition to the primary qualities, there are also secondary qualities in the celestial globes: lightness, heaviness, softness, hardness, thinning, and thickening. The habit of his whole body was composed of a garment hitherto exotic and unseen; for it was adorned with a wonderful texture in the shape of folded wings, such that almost no kind of color could be conceived or imagined in the mind that his feathers did not express. I, nearly lifeless at this unusual sight—one never before seen by human eyes—and fixed to the ground, was struck dumb; my hair stood on end, and my voice stuck in my throat. Then, with my heart throbbing and all my marrow growing stiff...

# The Ecstatic Journey #

Is such a vast space inhabited by humans? For I see that it almost reaches the pole of the earth on one side.

***Cosmiel:*** It is entirely so, no differently than the other parts of the globe, although by the inscrutable judgment of God it has not yet been discovered; it will, however, be discovered in its own century, whenever it shall seem fit to Divine Providence. I will discuss these matters with you more at length in our final conversation. Do you see 그 most brilliant region which lies immediately beneath the **Southern Pole** <note>original: *polo Australi*; the South Pole</note>?

***Theodidactus:*** I see it.

***Cosmiel:*** That is a most vast island, surrounded by the highest mountain crags vomiting perpetual fire; yet the region is so far from remaining uninhabited that it is instead protected by those fires from all the sterility and the intensity of the cold that anyone might imagine in this zone. You should consider that the same thing occurs in the region subject to the **North** <note>original: *plaga Boreæ*; the northern region or Arctic</note>.

***Theodidactus:*** But I ask you one thing more, Master, to explain: what is the meaning of that region near the **Caspian Sea**, which radiates with such unusual light?

***Cosmiel:*** You ask a wonderful thing, my son, but I do not know whether I ought to reveal such a great and significant matter to you. Indeed, no mortal has yet penetrated that region because of the inaccessible precipices of the rocky mountains arranged in a sort of crown; nor is it the will of God that this place be revealed except in the final days. At the beginning of the created world, the <term>First-Created</term> <note>original: *Protoplasti*; Adam and Eve, the first humans</note>, blessed with every happiness, inhabited this place. After they were finally expelled from there through sin, they left the place inaccessible to mortals. In later times, **Enoch** and **Elijah** were <margin>The Earthly Paradise.</margin> translated into this place to lead a life that is blessed and [removed] from all the [fragility] of human transience... <note>The text ends mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>

...they lead a life free from miseries, in the contemplation of divine things, until the time appointed for them by God. ***Theodidactus:*** Please, let it be so.

Here, the ridges of extremely high mountains—especially on the Moon’s circumference—and there, valleys, lakes, rivers, and seas were presented to my eyes on all sides. ***Cosmiel:*** My son, I will not only show these things to you from a distance, but so that you may see each and every thing up close, I will lead you onto the globe itself.

***Theodidactus:*** He had scarcely spoken, when...

The rock of the mountain was variegated with white, and was, as if by some untamable hardness, incorruptible <note>original: *incorruptibile*; in older science, celestial objects were thought to be made of "incorruptible" matter that never decays or changes, unlike objects on Earth</note>, adorned with various many-colored streaks. # On the Moon

<margin>Wonders of the Lunar Ocean.</margin> It surrounds the circumference of the lunar globe, and together with the Moon's rotation, it is driven in a circle with a perpetual course and flow. These movements occur most intensely when the ocean is struck by the **perpendicular influx** <note>original: "normali influxu." In 17th-century physics, "normal" refers to a right angle. Kircher is arguing that the Sun’s rays are most powerful when hitting the water directly at a 90-degree angle.</note> of the Sun's rays, which happens at the time of the full moon or the new moon. For as you heard above, lunar water is wonderfully mobile; thus, as soon as the Sun strikes it with a perpendicular diffusion of rays, the water is soon reduced to extreme **rarity** <note>original: "raritatem." Kircher follows the Aristotelian idea that heat "thins" or expands water, causing it to take up more space and thus move violently—his explanation for tides.</note>, causing those vehement agitations both at the time of the full moon on the side facing us, and at the time of the new moon on the far side. 

From this, while the water of the Lunar Ocean is agitated, it is dashed quite violently both against the opposing rocks and against the walls of the vast mountains—of which, as you see, there is no number. It is inevitable that a horrific agitation is caused there by these contrary motions. Added to the extreme mobility of the unstable lunar element is the daily motion of the Sun, by which the sea, having been pushed, acquires forces that are greater the more perpendicular the position of the sea is to the Sun. From this also comes that formidable sound; for the dashing of waves, both against the opposing rocks and against themselves, causes a certain wonderful agitation of the lunar air—or what is the same thing, the **lunar effluvium** <note>original: "Lunaris effluuij." Kircher uses this to describe the lunar atmosphere or the "exhalations" rising from its surface.</note>—from which that strange and unusual sound is produced. For you know from the similarity of terrestrial things that troubled water can by no means coexist with the stillness of air.

***Theodidactus:*** But I ask you, please, for what purpose did the supreme <term>Architect of the World</term> <note>original: "Mundi Opifex." A common Latin title for God as the craftsman or builder of the universe.</note> ordain such great agitations of the waters on the Moon? 

***Cosmiel:*** The most powerful purpose is so...

<margin>A day of fourteen days on the Moon.</margin>

### ->On the Moon<-

...why do we not see similar things on the Moon as we do when situated on the Earth?

<margin>Why clouds are not seen on the Moon.</margin>

*Cosmiel*: My son, you heard earlier that the Lunar waters, due to their thinness <note>original: "exilitatem," referring here to a lack of density or substance compared to Earth's water</note>, are not sufficient to form clouds, rain, or hail. Instead, the Moon abounds with bright vapors, as you can see here before you. Although these wander across the face of the Moon, they cannot obscure it, as they are incapable of opacity. However, the clouds of the terrestrial globe <note>the Earth</note>, because they are formed from the watery element filled with a great deal of "earthly mixture" <note>minerals or particles that make the vapors dense and dark</note>, are easily lifted high by the colder surrounding air. Then, by the design of provident Nature, they are either condensed into opaque clouds, frozen into hail, or melted into necessary rains, without which the mechanism of the terrestrial world <note>original: "Mundi machina"</note> could not function.

*Theodidactus*: I understand it all. But tell me, I ask, what are those fiery globes that I see around the horizon of the Moon? Sometimes I see them with two horns <note>crescent-shaped</note>, sometimes halved <note>original: "dichotomos," referring to the quarter-phase</note>, and now full?

*Cosmiel*: That one which you see further from the horizon is the globe of Venus; the other is the globe of Mercury. 

<margin>How Venus and Mercury appear from the Moon.</margin>

*Theodidactus*: But why do they appear to be of such unusual size? I would truly swear they were two Moons!

*Cosmiel*: The reason is that both have reached their closest proximity to the Moon within their orbits at this time. Both are at aphelion <note>original: "aphelius," the point in an orbit furthest from the Sun; in the geocentric model used here, this brings them closer to the outer planetary spheres</note>. In this way, it happens that the further they are removed from the Sun, the closer they present themselves to the Moon on that side where the aphelia of the Sun, Venus, and Mercury coincide with the Moon's own aphelion. Consequently, the laws of optics teach that they appear in a much larger form. Furthermore, since those two are spherical bodies which receive no light from themselves but only from the Sun...

# ->Ecstatic Journey<-

<margin><unclear>How</unclear> <unclear>the Moon</unclear> <unclear>is sustained.</unclear></margin>
...how does the Moon remain stable in that immense ocean of the ethereal expanse? Perhaps you fear the Moon might fall? <term>Theodidactus</term> <note>The fictional student in this dialogue; his name means "God-taught."</note>: Since I see no support upon which it might lean, nor do I see it fixed to a solid sphere—as the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, who believed the heavens were composed of solid, crystalline spheres that carried the planets.</note> ridiculously imagine for themselves—I am rightly afraid. <term>Cosmiel</term> <note>The angelic guide representing divine knowledge.</note>, cease your fear; pay attention to what I am about to reveal to you. The Creator of the World, in His infinite wisdom, when in the first infancy of the world He separated innumerable systems of worldly bodies from that immense <term>chaos</term> <note>The formless matter that existed before the universe was ordered.</note>, endowed them with such powers and properties that, although they were all fashioned from one and the same mixture of elements, they do not therefore agree in their properties and powers.
<margin>All celestial bodies differ by reason of their constitution.</margin>
Rather, they are constituted with as many diverse qualities and properties as there are diverse things in the world (of which there is no number); and this was done to show the glory, power, wisdom, and uncomprehended majesty of the Creator in His creatures. Furthermore, although all the systems of worldly globes are diverse in themselves, it has been so arranged by the incomprehensible disposition of divine wisdom that there is no body, however small, that does not flow into the unity of the whole and conspire toward the universal preservation of the world. Since the body of the Moon is such, you should not wonder that the Moon remains stable in the ethereal space by its own power, leaning on no support; for at such and such a distance from the earth, and in such a position, it has been allotted its own center, in which it can most aptly carry out its duty of exerting influence; and since that center [is distant/different] from the center of the Earth...

<summary>In this passage, Cosmiel explains to Theodidactus that the Moon does not fall despite the lack of solid spheres because God endowed every celestial body with unique properties and a specific place in the universal order. The text rejects the Aristotelian idea of solid planetary spheres in favor of a universe where bodies are sustained by divine geometry and internal "virtue."</summary>

There they preserve themselves, and there they work together for the preservation of this globe, so that the purpose for which it was made by the most wise Founder of all things might better fulfill its duty of influence <note>In 17th-century science, "influence" referred to the physical and astrological effects celestial bodies were believed to exert on the Earth.</note>. This **Lunar** globe therefore has its own center, so constant and stable that it is more necessary for the machine of the **World** to be dissolved than for it to fail the law dictated to it. <margin>The reason for the lunar phases is explained.</margin>
...[per]petually exposed to the solar rays, it might temper the heat of the Sun through the efficacy of its own moist power; and lest, by always striking the surface of the earth with the same face, it might overwhelm the earth with an abundance of its **swelling moisture** <note>original: "humoris sui tumefactivi." Early modern science held that the Moon's primary influence was "moistening," which caused tides to rise and biological tissues to swell.</note>, it turns its face toward the terrestrial globe in such a way that it is not always full, nor half, but by a certain successive decrease or increase of its light, now completely lacking light, now increased with resumed strength, it might diminish the abundance of the moisture it has drawn in, or repair its deficiency by a proportionate increase of light. Thus the Moon is so constituted that, in the course of a month's space, it turns as much of its dark face toward us as it does of its bright face; for just as at the **full moon** <note>original: "plenilunio."</note> it turns its entire face imbued with light toward us, so at the time of the **new moon** <note>original: "novilunij."</note> it turns the entirety of its dark face. In this way, during the **quadratures** <term>quadratures: the phases (first and last quarters) when the Moon is at a 90-degree angle from the Sun, appearing exactly half-illuminated to an observer on Earth.</term>, it offers us half light and half darkness equally; likewise, in the **sextile aspect** <term>sextile aspect: an astronomical position where two celestial bodies are 60 degrees apart. Here, Kircher is using it to describe the proportions of light and shadow during the crescent phases.</term>, it exhibits as much darkness to us as it shows light in the **gibbous** <note>original: "tuberosa." Literally "tuberous" or "swelling," this refers to the phase where the Moon is more than half but less than fully illuminated.</note> face of the bright Moon, so that, as if by partitioned laws, it might preserve the earthly body in its vigor through an equal proportion of light, darkness, heat, and cold, of **rarefaction** <term>rarefaction: the process by which a substance becomes less dense, usually through the application of heat.</term> and **condensation** <term>condensation: here meaning the thickening or strengthening of matter through cooling.</term>; for what the light of the Moon dissolves on earth, this the cold [of its dark side] binds by its influence; what the light scatters, the cold gathers again; what the light weakens with its excessive warmth, the cold preserves from decay.

# Of the Ecstatic Journey

...the very form itself finally diverges; the reason for which is nothing other than the disparate condition of the positions of the parts of the Earth, and the greater or lesser force and efficacy of the Sun perpetually striking the Earth. If, therefore, such a great transformation of things occurs within the circuit of the terrestrial Zones <note>The "Zones" refer to the classical division of the Earth into frigid, temperate, and torrid regions based on climate</note>, how great a change do you think occurs in the celestial bodies, which differ by the whole of heaven?

Gird up your loins, therefore, and whatever unusual and admirable things you shall see, or hear explained by me, I wish for you to hide them away in the depths of your heart. ## *Concerning the journey from the Moon to the globe of Venus.*

**T**HEODIDACTUS. Oh my most beloved *Cosmiel*, what do I see? <margin>The transport of Theodidactus to the globe of Venus.</margin>

Because of this, you are moved not of your own accord, but by my work, as if toward its center; and now, as you see, we have almost reached our destination. *Theodidactus:* Oh my *Cosmiel*, what a marvelous appearance of things I behold! How great the vastness of this globe, how many shining rocks I see! *Cosmiel*, a little later you will see greater things. *Theodidactus:* With this said, [he placed] me onto the very land of Venus...

<margin>The nature of the night.</margin>
...arises only from an illusion of your eye, which—when you are positioned on a ship progressing with however fast a motion—imagines that the shores are moving rather than the ship. But since these things are well-known to you, I will not dwell on them further; instead, receive these few words concerning the brevity of the night. Since the rays of the Sun graze this globe (which is twice as small as the Earth and closer to the Sun) across the greatest part of its circumference, and only a tiny, dark portion is left on the face turned away from the Sun, it is inevitable that the night is very short and the darkness barely exceeds that of twilight. This is due both to the supreme clarity of the air—illuminated by the reflection from the **crystalline mountains** <note>Kircher describes Venus as being composed of translucent, gem-like rocks that amplify light.</note>—and to the very rapid rotation of the entire globe around its own axis. Finally, it is due to the proximity and size of the Moon, which illuminates it from the opposite side by performing the deputy role of the Sun. Thus, upon this globe, a nearly continuous day appears without night, even when the Sun is positioned in the opposite signs of the zodiac.

### Journey to the globe of the Sun.

Have you ever seen a wheel on which knives are usually sharpened? If you pour water over it while it is being agitated with a vehement motion, <insert>Am...</insert> the water does not follow the wheel, but being lifted upward by the violence of the impetus, it is dissipated into the air. You ought to think that the same would happen to the globe of the Sun, if it were composed of pure liquid; for while the Solar body is revolved from the east to the west around the globe of the Earth <note>Kircher is describing the daily motion of the Sun from a geocentric perspective, which was still a common framework for Jesuit astronomers in the 17th century.</note> in the space of a natural day, unless it were restrained by certain more solid particles like barriers <term>repagulis</term> <note>original: "repagulis," meaning bars, bolts, or restraints.</note>, it could by no means remain stable. Indeed, it would necessarily happen that by the excessive violence of the motion by which the said liquid globe is driven into a circle by its daily rotation, it would either be dissipated or, with its power dispersed and confused, it would create an entirely chaotic and strange appearance for the globe. Since the fervor of the matter is endowed with a waving and extreme mobility, the Sun—on account of its excessive rapidity—would be drawn now into an oval, now into a **Rhomboid**, and now into some other shape perceptible to the eye; yet you know this is contrary to experience.

<margin>
Why God enclosed the fiery sea of the Sun within channels.
</margin>

Therefore, so that this great inconsistency in the nature of things does not hinder the operations of its influential power, nature—the provident moderator of all things—enclosed this fiery liquid within the channels <note>original: "alueos" (alveos), referring to conduits or beds like those of a river.</note> of more solid parts, so that being restrained as if in some truly wonderful vessel, it might not exceed the limits of its own heat. From this you see that the Northern as well as the Southern parts for the most part, as well as the depths of the Solar body, are provided with more solid parts like a certain skeleton <term>ossatura</term> <note>Kircher uses this term to describe a "bonework" or structural frame that gives the Sun its permanent spherical shape.</note> proportioned to the whole globe, which contains within itself, as if in a womb, the matter of the shining liquid.

The fiery vapors, however, having been carried on high and continually following the impetus of the Sun's motion, are now purified from their fiery moisture and expand into huge clouds by their own thinness; then they are again scattered into smaller portions until at last, attracted by the <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "virtute." <margin>How the globe exerts its latent powers.</margin>
...the flow of fluid matter is driven toward its destined ends; for, as we discussed above regarding the solar globe, it is impossible for a globe to exert its appropriate power toward the end for which the Architect of Nature <note>Latin: *Opifex* — a term Kircher uses to describe God as the supreme craftsman or engineer of the universe.</note> instilled it into the globe, except through continuous motion, and specifically a motion of circulation. Since the entire globe acts upon the lower regions by its influential power, the whole could not act if it exhaled its power only at the surface level; and thus the internal constitution of the central parts would seem to have been established by nature in vain. <margin>The element of fire in individual globes corresponds to the nature of the entire globe.</margin>
...taken radically, it is properly and essentially elementary fire. For, as you have heard, terrestrial fire reflects the nature, odor, and color of those bodies which provide it with nourishment <note>Latin: *alimentum* — fuel or sustenance for the fire.</note>; solar fire, being most bright and pure, follows the nature of its own most pure substance. Here, Martian fire likewise tastes of the nature of the Martian matter from which it receives its nourishment, and so it is with the others. Hence you see it full of things like soot, and imbued with a varied mixture of bitumen and pitch-like matter. However, all these different types of fire have this in common by their very nature: they are hot, penetrating, and perpetually surging.

<margin>The nature of the watery element in the globe of Mars.</margin>
The liquid of this Martian sea exhibits the watery element, although it is very different from the moisture of the other globes. It is sluggish, filthy, confused, and polluted by a vast mixture of material variety. Yet, if someone using the **chemical art** <note>Latin: *chimica arte* — referring to alchemy or early chemistry.</note> were to place it in an <term>alembic</term> <note>A specialized vessel used in distillation to separate substances by heating and cooling.</note> and separate the pure from the impure, he would undoubtedly find a watery moisture not much different from that of the Earth, the Moon, and the rest.

<margin>Martian air.</margin>
Martian air relates to the globe of Mars just as terrestrial air relates to the terrestrial globe, and as solar air relates to the Sun, or lunar air to the Moon. Since air is nothing other than a kind of specific <term>effluvium</term> <note>original: *efflauium* — a vaporous exhalation or outflow.</note> of any globe mixed with the <term>ether</term> <note>The subtle fluid believed to fill the space between celestial bodies.</note>, it is certainly necessary that the air tastes of the nature of the globe from which it is breathed out. Although by its own nature it is fluid and highly mobile, just like the terrestrial, solar, or lunar air, these nevertheless differ among themselves so much that it would be impossible for a person to live in the air of any of the mentioned globes, except in that...

...which the Creator assigned for its respiration, namely, to live naturally in the terrestrial manner. <margin>The Earthly element in the globe of Mars, <term>♂</term> <note>The astronomical and alchemical symbol for Mars.</note></margin> The stony mass of this globe expresses the earthly element to you, although this too differs from the terrestrial element by qualities as wide as the heavens. For as you see, it consists of the hardest stones and crags: sulfur, arsenic, **orpiment** <note>Latin: *auripigmentum* — a deep-colored, orange-yellow arsenic sulfide mineral once used as a pigment.</note>, antimony, and iron-bearing masses and rocks, which in appearance are not at all dissimilar to our own minerals. If these stones were resolved into their first principles by the **chemical art** <note>Referring to alchemy or early chemistry.</note>, they would leave behind a dust that is almost identical to terrestrial dust in terms of its bare substance. Thus you have here the four elements—not indeed in an earthly condition, but Martian, according to the condition of the globe of Mars. From this you may clearly gather that the diverse qualities of the elements considered thus far have no other cause for such great diversity than the various powers and properties of the globes with which they are imbued. Yet with this difference: that while there are 365 days which the Sun completes in its annual course according to its own motion, such Jovian days are equal to 4,550 of our days, which [Jupiter] completes in its own great eccentric <term>eccentric orbit</term> <note>original: "excentrico." In early astronomy, an eccentric was a circular orbit whose center was slightly offset from the Earth or Sun.</note> by its own motion according to the order of the signs, when a comparison is made to the Sun.

You should consider that you have traveled as much space as its diameter stretches; for this will be the diameter of the entire globe closest to Jupiter <note>This refers to the moon Io, the innermost of the four moons discovered by Galileo in 1610.</note>. The second globe is as far from the center of the Jovian globe as the space you would cover in 27,784 hourly leagues <note>An "hourly league" (leuca horaria) was a common unit of measurement in 17th-century science, roughly representing the distance a person could walk in one hour—approximately three miles or 4.8 kilometers.</note>; you may consider the diameter of this second globe to occupy about 822 leagues. The third globe is separated from the center of the Jovian globe by a space equal to six of Jupiter's diameters extended in length—namely, it would encompass a space of 41,676 hourly leagues—and if you travel 1,185 leagues across this third globe, you will know that you have measured its diameter. Finally, the fourth and outermost companion globe of Jupiter fills a space of ten Jovian diameters—that is, it is 69,460 hourly leagues distant from the center of Jupiter—on which, if you travel 1,736 leagues in a straight line, you should judge that you have traveled as much space as the entire length of its diameter occupies. From these measurements you may gather that the first is 6,946 leagues from the second; the second is 13,892 from the third; and the third is 27,784 hourly leagues distant from the fourth. 

And from these distances you will secondly gather that the first and smallest of all these four reviewed globes is almost equal to our Moon in the solidity and thickness of its mass, although to you, gazing at its visible diameter, it appears twice as large as the diameter of our Moon when viewed from the Earth. The second, indeed, easily equals the globe of Mercury in its mass; the third is not inferior to Venus in its mass; and the fourth, finally, is not much larger than the terrestrial globe <note>Kircher is attempting to harmonize the new telescopic discoveries of the moons of Jupiter with the known planets of the solar system, suggesting a "miniature solar system" where each moon corresponds in size to a planet (Moon, Mercury, Venus, and Earth). The movement of the four companions, and how they illuminate Jupiter?

...it is certain that the light of the first globe <note>the moon Io</note> sweeps across and surveys the surface of the Jovian globe twice as fast as the light of the Sun is accustomed to survey the surface <note>This refers to the rapid rotation of Jupiter, which completes a "day" in about 10 hours, making the moons appear to move very quickly across its sky</note>. And therefore, God the Best and Greatest, the creator of all things, so arranged the movements of the said globes that, by a most pleasant and perpetual alternation, as the light of the first globe escapes the Sun’s gaze too quickly, the light of the second would soon take its place; then the light of this third globe would follow; and finally, as this one sets, the light of the last globe would rise. 

From these facts, several things follow: 

First, that Jovian <term>days and nights</term> <note>Kircher uses "Jovian" to describe things pertaining to the planet Jupiter</note> are unequal, not so much in their total duration of time, but in the intensity of their light. For who can doubt that two, three, or even four of Jupiter's most brilliant globes rising at the same time bring more daylight and brightness to the planet than just one alone? 

Second, that for the duration of nearly two days in many Jovian regions—or rather, within the space of twenty-four hours—there would sometimes be night; specifically at that time when all the moons are joined together in <term>conjunction</term> <note>When the moons align on one side of the planet, leaving the opposite side in darkness</note>, occurring in those Jovian parts which are diametrically or nearly oppositely placed from such a conjunction. 

Third, it follows that more frequent eclipses occur among the Jovian globes than our own lunar eclipses, and these are quite remarkable, though they last for only a short time. 

And from all these things it is clearly evident why, since this vast globe of Jupiter could not be sufficiently illuminated by the Sun <note>Jupiter is much further from the Sun than Earth, receiving significantly less solar energy</note>, God associated it with these globes—acting as "deputy Suns," that is, globes of a <term>solar nature</term> <note>Kircher suggests the moons possess a subtle inherent light of their own, similar to the Sun, rather than just reflecting light like our Moon</note>—which, surrounding Jupiter like sentries on distributed watches, might regulate it with a wonderful alternation in that balance of light...

<margin>Explanation of the variety observed in them.</margin>

I revealed some of the causes of these appearances a little earlier; now the phenomena of the remaining ones must be explained to you. The reason these companions occasionally degenerate from a round into an oval form is the oblique position of the stars, through which they are viewed across the glassy atmosphere of Saturn. Since this medium resembles the terrestrial air and strongly refracts the bodies situated within it, it is through the force of this refraction—in almost the same way you see the Sun when it is near the horizon—that they deflect from a round shape into the likeness of an oval figure. 

But as for why they occasionally appear in the form of little handles, or a horned Moon, or rather in the form of crab's pincers <note>original: "forficibus cancri"</note> with which they seem to squeeze the globe of Saturn, the cause is that those spherical bodies, intercepted by the equally spherical body of Saturn, create such a cross-section as you see, which is clearly evident from the principles of optics. ***Theodidactus:*** You explain all things well indeed, but this troubles me: what to it-

# Journey to the globe of Saturn.

...[what] that dark emptiness means, which is interposed between Saturn and the horns of its companions? ***Cosmiel***: You ask a great thing, but lest I seem to fail your wishes, I shall teach you this. First, you must suppose that the globe of Saturn, no differently than the other globes of the world, revolves around its own axis. Second, you must suppose that the globe, as you see with your own eyes, surpasses all other worldly globes both in the ruggedness of its chained mountains and in the deformity of its sprawling masses. Third, the Saturnian body is surrounded by a certain sluggish liquid, not unlike mercury <note>original: "hydrargyro"; Kircher posits that Saturn is covered in a reflective, metallic fluid to explain its brightness despite its distance from the Sun</note>, which, as it is most brilliant, requires only the smallest light to be illuminated. Conversely, its terrestrial portions, due to the recesses of the valleys and the darkness of vast chasms, are not open to light except in a flickering or uncertain way. Whenever, therefore, the dark parts of Saturn coincide with the darker parts of the companions <note>the "companions" are the rings of Saturn, which early astronomers like Kircher believed were separate satellite bodies or physical attachments</note>, they will necessarily cause certain dark gaps or shadows in the middle. Meanwhile, the remaining portion of the companions, shining with its own light, passes into handled and horned phases <note>original: "ansatas et cornutas"; early telescopic views of Saturn's rings often looked like handles ("ansae") or crescent horns</note>, until finally one moves behind Saturn and the other moves to the opposite side, joined as if in a straight line with the body of Saturn, and they vanish from the eyes of those dwelling on Earth.

...if you place one light against another luminous body, would it suffer any eclipse from the meeting of that opposing bright body? ***Theodidactus:*** I believe it would suffer none. For if a lit candle is placed between a fire and my sight, experience teaches that the candle’s light, joined with the fire's light, presents the whole as a single luminous form. ***Cosmiel:*** So it is with these two globes, the companions of Saturn <note>Early astronomers, including Kircher, struggled to identify Saturn's rings, often describing them as "companions" (comites) or side-globes rather than a continuous disk.</note>. Even though the first one is placed between our eyes and Saturn’s body, it causes no eclipse. This is because the companions are bright by their own nature and, in fact, help to illuminate Saturn itself. Whenever a smaller luminous globe is joined with another larger illuminated one, they must necessarily be seen with their lights blended together as a single face of the larger illuminated globe. If, however, this companion globe were a purely opaque body without its own light, then it would certainly appear as a dark spot against Saturn’s illuminated globe. The fact that no such eclipse has ever been detected when the companions cross Saturn is a most brilliant proof that they shine with their own light.

<margin>The origin of the phases of Saturn’s companions.</margin>

From this you may also gather that the various phases of the companions arise only from their rotation around Saturn. When they are distant and separate, they appear round. At other times, when viewed through the dewy transparency of the atmosphere <note>Kircher often attributed the changing shapes of celestial bodies to "refraction" caused by the thick vapors or atmospheres he believed surrounded all planets.</note>, they are refracted into an oval shape. Sometimes, when partially obscured by Saturn’s globe, they take on a horned appearance, and when they are positioned directly in front of or behind Saturn, they vanish entirely. ***Theodidactus:*** A significant doubt still lingers in my mind regarding those handled <note>original: "ansulata"; referring to the "ansae" or handles that the rings appeared to form on either side of the planet in early telescopes.</note>...

# Journey to the Globe of Saturn #

...their crescent or horned appearance. ***Cosmiel:*** Your doubt is of no small importance. Therefore, so that it may be resolved, I wish you to know first that these globes—always positioned at an equal distance opposite one another, as was mentioned above—shine with their own light. This light does not come from their entire mass, but from a liquid igneous element <note>Kircher posits that celestial bodies are composed of the four elements; here, he explains the "glow" of Saturn's companions as a fluid layer of fire.</note> that surrounds a large part of these globes. Their terrestrial substance, however, being endowed with an opaque body, shuns the light and can by no means participate in it. 

<margin>The origin of the phases of Saturn’s companions.</margin>

Whenever, therefore, these globes are positioned in their orbit in such a way that their substance—partly terrestrial and partly luminous—meets the eyes of those on Earth, it is certain that the globes can only be viewed in the shape of "little handles" <term>ansulae (little handles)</term> <note>Early astronomers, unable to see the rings clearly, described the protrusions on either side of Saturn as "ansae" or handles.</note> or horns, since the stony part of their substance has nothing to illuminate it. However, when they are in that position of their orbit where, in their rotation around their own center, they turn their entire luminous part toward the Earth, then they will undoubtedly be seen as full of light and round. Thus, whatever Astronomy teaches you regarding the phases and eclipses of the Moon, you must judge the same to happen here—with the only exception being that the Moon shines with borrowed light <note>original: *alienâ... luce*</note>, while these shine with their own; and while the Moon only oscillates, these are carried around their own center, as I have said.

**Theodidactus:** I have understood everything perfectly; indeed, from this visual experience, I feel as though I can almost touch the truth of the matter with my own fingers. Furthermore, nothing remains but for you to explain to me how these globes illuminate Saturn. 

**Cosmiel:** First, it must be noted that the globe of Saturn, if it does not exceed the globe of Jupiter in size, at least equals it. <margin>How these two companions illuminate Saturn.</margin>

For this reason, nature has provided it with two other "deputy suns"—that is, bodies of a solar nature—lest this massive worldly globe seem to have been created in vain, lacking sufficient light and heat. These are the two globes which, like two deputy suns <note>original: "vicarij Soles"; Kircher interprets the protrusions of Saturn (the rings) as independent light-giving bodies.</note>, both rotate around their own centers and orbit Saturn at a constant distance from one another, so that no part of the giant globe remains without the benefit of their light. Therefore, by a clever arrangement of nature, the globe of Saturn not only rotates on its own axis, but also "nods" <note>original: "nutet"; Kircher is describing axial tilt or nutation, the wobbling motion that allows different parts of a planet to face its light source.</note> somewhat toward opposite parts of the world. ## CHAPTER IX.

### *Concerning the journey into the Region of the firmament or the fixed stars.*

<margin>Theodidactus burns with desire to see the solid sphere of the fixed stars.</margin>
**THEODIDACTUS.** Where are you snatching me, Cosmiel? Where am I being carried with such ineffable velocity of motion? What, finally, is the destination of my journey? Where now is the Sun, where the Earth, the Moon, and the other planets? Indeed, I see they have all disappeared. Is it possible that we have covered so much space in such a short time?

**Cosmiel.** Do not wonder, for you are being carried not by human but by angelic motion; in comparison to which every motion of natural things is mere slowness. Nor could you sustain this impetus unless you were strengthened from on high. 

**Theodidactus**: And when at last shall we reach that crystalline mass of the firmament <term>firmamentum; in traditional cosmology, the "firmament" was the shell of the universe that held the stars in place</term>? When shall we behold that immense sphere of fixed stars, closed by no boundaries? And how shall we penetrate the most solid mass of such an immense body, which is like "molten bronze" <note>original: "tanquam ære fusi." This is a reference to the Book of Job 37:18, describing the sky as a strong, molten mirror.</note>? Let us hurry, I ask, so that we may more closely behold the supreme handiwork of the infinite wisdom of God, the Best and Greatest. For I burn with great desire to see by what craftsmanship those stars, which we call "fixed" <note>Stars are called "fixed" because, unlike the "wandering" planets, they remain in the same position relative to one another in the constellations.</note>, are fixed to that crystalline sphere <term>chrystallinum orbem; the transparent, solid celestial sphere of ancient and medieval astronomy</term> of incomprehensible vastness. By what diligence are they inserted into it? With what light do they shine? With what property do they excel? Is the matter of that sphere essentially different from elementary matter <note>original: "materia elementari." The four elements (earth, water, air, fire) were thought to exist only below the moon; the heavens were traditionally believed to be made of a fifth element, the "quintessence" or "aether."</note>...

### Journey into the Firmament

If the Earth, the Sun, or the Moon were viewed from this solar body of the firmament; and if your Sun, when seen from this location in the firmament, appeared with a diameter of no more than three minutes <note>A "minute" here refers to an arcminute, a unit used by astronomers to measure the apparent size of objects in the sky. You see, therefore, from this reasoning, that it is impossible <note>original Greek: *αδύνατον* (adynaton)</note> for the Sun to illuminate these globes of the firmament that are diametrically opposite to it. <margin>Unless many bodies of a solar nature had been established, the world would have perished in darkness.</margin>

It was therefore necessary for many bodies of a solar nature to be established, which would illuminate the globes closer to them, so that a large portion of the world would not be deprived of necessary light. <margin>The various motions of the stars.</margin>

In this vast expanse of ethereal breeze, the **Architect** <note>A title for God emphasizing his role as the master builder of the universe.</note> of the world arranged this collection of innumerable globes in relation to the position of the terrestrial globe <note>The Earth</note> in such a way that each and every one begins its motion from the east toward the west. By a perennial law of stability, they continue these motions around the earth according to the immutable decrees of the divine Idea. [Light] was most necessary to the world, seeing that without it the world could not have existed, condemned to eternal darkness; thus, it had to precede the appearance of all other forms. # Of the Creation of the World

<margin>The extraordinary purpose of the terrestrial globe.</margin>
...of the Creator; then the Terrestrial globe, in which he was to create the human race according to his image and likeness; for the material world would have seemed to be created in vain, if there were no rational, physical creature who might behold the power and majesty of the divine works. By beholding them, he might wonder at them; and by wondering, he might seek after the **Craftsman** <note>original: "Opificem," referring to God as the architect or builder of the universe</note> of such great power; and having sought Him, he might love Him, and finally enjoy Him forever. Therefore the Earth, as the superior part of the world for whose sake all other things were created, had to be named first; while the other globes, destined to serve it, were mentioned only implicitly. The terrestrial globe is like a certain **prototype** <note>original: "prototypon"</note> of the others; whence, on account of the purpose for which it was destined, it is deservedly the most excellent of all the worldly globes, and equipped with a greater abundance and variety of all things necessary for human life. <margin>The excellence of the terrestrial globe.</margin> For the other globes, as servants, were equipped chiefly with those natural gifts which were necessary for them to achieve the goal intended by God. ### On the Creation of the World

In fact, all things are present in act <term>act (actus): the state of being fully realized or "active" in reality</term> within the Mind from eternity, and they will always remain within it supersubstantially <note>original: "supersubstantialiter"; meaning in a way that transcends the nature of physical substance or essence</note>. These three—God, the Angel, and matter—are "whole" from the beginning and will always be "whole"; they can neither be renewed nor multiplied, nor can they perish or be diminished. The human intellect, however, can indeed be multiplied, and it is not "whole" from the beginning, as it is perfected in its total number day by day, until it emerges entirely into act and the human species is fulfilled; yet it can never be diminished.

# The Ecstatic Journey

<margin>Nothing can ascend toward perfection unless it first goes beyond its own degree.</margin>
<margin>Everything in the world enjoys a certain uniqueness.</margin>

...the Universe. You see, therefore, that different <term>species</term> <note>Categories of living things.</note> of a higher or lower <term>genus</term> <note>A broader classification than species.</note> are not joined together in some individual that does not admit of "more" or "less"; nor does a species descend so low as to be the absolute minimum of a genus, because before it reaches that minimum, it changes into another species before it can be the least. In the genus of animals, while the human species strives to reach the highest degree among sensing beings, it is caught up into a mixture with <term>intellectual nature</term> <note>The realm of pure reason and spirit, associated with angels or the divine mind.</note>; so much so that there is nothing in the Universe that does not enjoy a certain <term>uniqueness</term> <note>original: "singularitate." ...[pro]portion of its due size <note>original: "portione magnitudinis debita," completing a sentence from the previous page regarding the Moon's size and distance</note>, so that if, by divine power, its distance from both the Sun and the Earth and its size were changed, all harmony would necessarily be thrown into confusion, and the Earth would inevitably perish. For at its specific distance, it can aptly nourish the Earth with its influence, and at no other; likewise at that same specific distance, and no other, it can mitigate the heat of the Sun. Conversely, the Sun can so temper the Moon’s moisture <note>original: "humiditatem." In the science of the time, the Moon was thought to be naturally "cold and wet," providing a necessary balance to the Sun's "hot and dry" nature.</note> and coldness by the mixture of its own rays that it produces the effect intended by nature to be bestowed upon the Earth. 

For if the Moon were closer to the Earth, it would produce entirely discordant and inconsistent effects on the Earth through its excessive moisture. On the other hand, if it were closer to the Sun, the Sun would act more powerfully upon the Moon, consuming its moisture and destroying everything in the terrestrial world with its excessive heat. Thus, nature set the watery Lunar body against the fiery Solar body at such a proportional distance so that one might restrain the other's force upon the Earth, binding and tying them together like a discord joined to a harmony. 

Because the Sun does not always strike the Earth with the same heat, but varies according to its annual and daily ascent and descent, nature likewise did not wish the Moon to always strike the Earth with the same degree of moisture and coldness. Instead, this varies according to the different alterations of the lunar phases <note>original: "phasium," referring to the changing appearance of the Moon from new to full</note>, as well as the manner of its ascent and descent in its apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit where a celestial body is furthest from the Earth</term> and perigee <term>perigee: the point in an orbit where a celestial body is closest to the Earth</term>. Thus, you see that in the hottest summer, the full Moon, being at its lowest and smallest, has little power; conversely, in the freezing winter, when the Sun is positioned in a low place, the full Moon as if... <note>The text ends mid-word "veluti," which means "as if" or "just as."</note>

# On the speed of the motion of the spheres

...by which, without any obstacle such as usually arises from the thickness of the air, they traverse immense terrestrial spaces most swiftly, even if this is not evident to the eyes because of the distance.

<margin>The **Copernicans** <note>original: *Copernicei*</note> falsely established the firmament as immobile, because they were unable to comprehend its speed.</margin>

**Theodidactus:** I have understood everything perfectly, and now I cannot marvel enough that many of the moderns <note>Refers to early modern scientists and astronomers, specifically those following Nicolaus Copernicus.</note>, driven astray by I know not what rashness—since they cannot comprehend such great speed of the **fixed stars** so as to be capable of understanding the divine work—have established the **fixed stars** as immobile, but the **Earth** as mobile? Is this not to prescribe limits to divine power? And to distort and adapt an incomprehensible work to the capacity of their own intellect? As if indeed **God, the Best and Greatest** <note>original: *Deus Optimus Maximus*</note> could produce nothing unless it squared in every way with their own genius; nor do they stop here; rather, they defend their error with such persistence that they are not ashamed to presumptuously drag even the very pages of the **Divine Word** <note>A reference to the Bible; critics of Copernicus often cited scripture to argue that the Earth stands still and the Sun moves.</note> and their meanings toward their own opinion, whether they like it or not. But now I proceed to another doubt: Why do the stars seen scattered around us from this sphere of the **firmament** feign such diverse motions?

<margin>The cause of the diversity of motion in the stars of the **firmament**.</margin>

Just as they have been assigned such and such a seat in the ethereal expanse, it is impossible for them to ever withdraw from it by even a tiny bit. You know how the Earth <note>original: Tellus</note> stands fixed by its center, suspended in the ethereal space? What power of the winds do you think could be so great as to move it from its divinely appointed seat? Surely none. I would like you to feel the same about each and every body in the world. Hence it is no wonder they can never be torn from their seats; therefore, they are always seen to maintain the same distance from one another, at least in appearance. I said "in appearance," because even if the individual globes—no differently than the planets <note>original: Planetae</note>—have different motions and complete their periods in peculiar circles for the reasons mentioned previously, nevertheless, these circles within which they perform their motions are entirely imperceptible <note>original: insensibiles</note> due to the excessive distance from the Earth. 

<margin>The circles or paths in which the fixed stars revolve would not be seen because of the excessive distance from the Earth; they are contracted into a point.</margin>
If, therefore, some star in its own particular circle were in conjunction with another star, or in opposition, or in a square configuration <term>square configuration|An astrological aspect where two celestial bodies are 90 degrees apart, often considered a point of tension.</term>, I will not say that such an appearance could be seen; rather, it entirely vanishes because of that difference of incredible distance I mentioned. The entire circle is contracted into an imperceptible point, in which nothing other than a point of light is seen, and no difference in position can be observed within it.

### *On the harmony of this sensible world, and its analogy with the rational, political, intellectual, and Archetypal world, and how each flows into the others.*

<margin>All things consist of three.</margin>
**C**OSMIEL. To God properly belongs the Monad or unity; to Mind or Wisdom belongs order or weight; and to the Soul or Spirit belongs measure and motion. Plato’s enigmatic pronouncement to King Dionysius beautifully explains this: *All things are around the King of all, and all things are for his sake, and he is the cause of all beautiful things.* <note>original: "Circa omnium Regem cuncta sunt..."; a famous passage from the Second Letter attributed to Plato, which Renaissance thinkers interpreted as a pre-Christian insight into the Trinity.</note> For all things are connected around the King by his unity, and all things are weighed for his sake, and all things are ordered toward him; and he himself, by numbering and proportioning all things, is the cause of all beauty—both efficient and final—as well as the governing and sustaining principle, the beginning, the middle, and the end of all. As Dionysius, the servant of God <note>original: "Dionysio seruo Dei"; referring again to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</note>, bears witness, from him...

# CHAPTER VIII.
