->### Of the Empyrean Heaven<-

...I have desired to see it, driven by I know not what pious affection and impulse. 

**Cosmiel:** Look, you are now restored to your place; proceed to propose the doubts that remain to you. 

**Theodidactus:** Is the Empyrean heaven composed of matter and form?

<margin>Whether it is composed of matter and form.</margin>

**Cosmiel:** Since I have said above that the Empyrean is a constitutive part of the world, it must necessarily be corporeal; if it is corporeal, it certainly will not be anything other than a physical body. Every <term>physical body (corpus physicum): in Aristotelian philosophy, a substance that exists in the natural world and is subject to change</term> is composed of matter and form; therefore, the Empyrean heaven is composed of matter and form. 

If anyone were to deny this, he would likewise be forced to deny all the qualities belonging to a physical and quantitative body. He would therefore be forced to admit that the Empyrean is affected by no visible qualities of colors, no audible qualities, no hardness, softness, condensation, rarefaction, or quantity. Thus, it would be entirely invisible, spiritual, and reachable only by the intellect—which everyone can see is absurd and contrary to the purpose of the most wise Creator <note>original: "Conditoris" — literally the Founder or Builder</note>. 

You must know this, however: the form and matter from which it is composed—and thus the whole composite—is constituted of parts that are, so to speak, infinitely more noble, excellent, and subtle, and of a more sublime form than those which make up all other bodies of the world. This is because the most benevolent Creator willed it to be endowed with the most eminent qualities and prerogatives for the pleasure and eternal delight of His Chosen <note>original: "Electorum" — referring to the "Elect," those souls destined for salvation and eternal life in heaven</note>. I shall say no more; of what sort and how great this [dwelling] of God Himself, the Angels, and...

<meta>catchword: blessed (Latin: beatorum)</meta>

<summary>In this passage, Cosmiel explains that the Empyrean heaven is a physical, "corporeal" place composed of matter and form, rather than a purely spiritual abstraction. He argues that it must have physical properties to be a real part of the universe, though its matter is of a much more refined and "noble" quality than that of the earthly realm.</summary>

Saint Paul clearly demonstrates the dwelling place of the blessed minds in his Epistle: *eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what things God has prepared for those who love Him* <note>original: "oculus non vidit, nec auris audiuit, nec in cor hominis ascendit, quæ Deus præparauit diligentibus se" — 1 Corinthians 2:9</note>. Truly, it seemed incongruous that this heaven—which was intended to receive a <term>rational creature (rationalem creaturam): a being endowed with reason, specifically a human being</term> composed of both soul and body—should have been created as purely spiritual or intellectual without a body. Therefore, it had to be corporeal, so that while the soul is absorbed in the contemplation of its Creator <note>original: "Conditoris"</note>, the body might also find an object proportioned to the delight of the senses, lest it seem to have been taken up into eternal glory in vain.

<margin>
Whether it is round or square.
</margin>
**Theodidactus:** Is the Empyrean heaven enclosed in a circle or a square? For many of the Holy Fathers, following the description of the <term>Evangelical Eagle (Euangelicæ Aquilæ): a traditional title for St. John the Apostle, whose Gospel and Revelation are said to soar to the heights of divinity</term> in the Apocalypse, maintain that its exterior surface is square; for thus it is said: *The city is set upon a square* <note>original: "Ciuitas supra quadratum posita est" — a reference to Revelation 21:16</note>.

**Cosmiel:** I would not have you understand these things literally, but rather persuade yourself that they are to be understood in an allegorical sense. Indeed, it signifies the supreme firmness and stability of this domicile, which lasts forever without any corruption or dissolution. However, it is bounded in a certain manner that is incomprehensible to the human mind; therefore, it would be in vain for me to explain it to you in more extensive words, since you cannot grasp it as long as you are weighed down by the <insert>burden of human mortality</insert>.

How vast the Empyrean heaven is.
</margin>
**Theodidactus:** Is the Empyrean heaven as vast as the Holy Fathers describe? 

**Cosmiel:** It is so; just as it encloses the entire <term>machine of the world (mundi machinam): the physical structure of the universe as a complex, God-designed system</term>, so it is worthily the [greatest] of all...

# CHAPTER IX.
### *Concerning imaginary space.*

<margin>The human mind cannot comprehend the infinite or the nothing.</margin>
**T**HEODIDACTUS. We have finally arrived at the ultimate boundary of the world; so that nothing remains except for you to explain to me what lies beyond the final limit of this <term>Empyrean Heaven (Empyrei Coeli): the highest, most spiritual part of the universe, believed to be the dwelling place of God</term>. Indeed, some philosophers mention a certain "imaginary space" outside the world, the nature of which no one is able to explain. Since the machine of the corporeal world—as you skillfully taught me earlier—cannot be infinite, what then can my mind conceive beyond the final boundary of all creation? Is it nothing? Is it some <term>being of reason (ens rationis): a concept that exists only in the mind rather than in external reality</term>? Is it a certain vacuum extended into infinity? 

*Cosmiel*. The human mind, accustomed as it is to things perceived by the senses, is as unable to conceive of "nothingness" as it is of the infinite. Therefore, so that you may be introduced somewhat into the <term>inner sanctums (adyta): the innermost, most sacred parts of a temple, used here to describe deep philosophical mysteries</term> of this profound speculation, I will begin from a slightly higher point. You ask what is after the final boundary of all creation? I answer: besides God, there is nothing. 

*Theodidactus*: What then is this "nothing"? 

*Cosmiel*. Nothing is nothing; for this is its adequate definition. 

*Theodidactus*: You are talking nonsense—if I may say so with your permission, my Cosmiel. 

*Cosmiel*.

->Tu-<- <note>original: "Tu-" — this is a catchword, indicating the first syllable of the next page.</note>

Then do you say the Master of eternal truth trifles?

*Theodidactus:* I beg you to forgive my rashness; that word escaped me, not because I judged you to be trifling—you who hold all the treasures of knowledge and wisdom hidden within your breast—but because among us men, born and raised in the shadows of ignorance, a definition of this sort could seem like a mere trifle. I promise that in the future I will stand by your judgment in whatever you say; therefore, please proceed.

<margin>Definition of nothing.</margin>
*Cosmiel:* I say, therefore, that Nothing is nothing other than nothing. I limit and define nothing by <term>non-being (non ente): that which does not exist in any form</term>, by nothingness, and by itself. For "nothing" is nothing; "nothing" is not "something." It is not this, or that, or any other <term>being (ens): a philosophical term for anything that exists</term>, but rather it is no being at all. Nothing is nowhere; it is not in the mind, nor in the nature of things, nor in the <term>intelligible world (intelligibili mundo): the realm of pure thought and ideas</term>, nor in the <term>sensible world (sensibili mundo): the physical world we perceive with our senses</term>, nor in God, nor outside of God in any creatures. Everything is a "being," everything is "something"; all things are full of being; nothing is idle, no vacuum is nothing, nothing is empty; "nothing" is exiled from the universe.

Whence, by the power of nature, *nothing comes from nothing* <note>original: "ex nihilo nihil fit"</note>. For, by the power of nature, something would be said to be made from nothing only if that which is simply and purely nothing were turned into being, or into matter, or into this "something"; or if that for which no beginning pre-existed, and for which no <term>potentiality (potentia): the inherent capacity for something to become reality</term> previously subsisted, were to proceed toward being something through some unusual miracle of nature. For whatever we see being made by nature, all of it is made from pre-existing matter, potentiality, and the <term>privation (privatione): the absence of a form or quality that should naturally be present</term> of itself; for its potentiality and matter subsisted before. It was begun from the begin—

<summary>Cosmiel defines "nothingness" as a total absence of being that exists neither in the mind, nor in God, nor in the physical world, reinforcing the Aristotelian principle that nature cannot create something out of nothing.</summary>
<keywords>nothingness, non-being, potentiality, privation, scholastic philosophy, ex nihilo nihil fit, Cosmiel, Theodidactus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the angel Cosmiel and the student Theodidactus. It completes the sentence from the previous page regarding the "beginning" (initio) of things and addresses the theological problem of creation "ex nihilo" (out of nothing).</meta>

<page-num>384</page-num>

...origin, and confused in the shadow of matter, whatever is perfected daily through continuous generations. 

*Theodidactus:*
<margin>How God produced all things out of nothing.</margin>
But how is God said to have produced all things out of nothing? 

*Cosmiel:* God cannot fall away from himself, God cannot be divided from God, and God cannot be taken separately and outside of God. Whatever is divine is God—joined and united with God—and is inseparable from himself and <term>indivisible (imparticibilis): that which cannot be broken into parts</term>. For if he were to become <term>partible (participabilis): capable of being shared out or divided</term>, a part of him would be taken outside the whole or outside another part. That part would therefore be divided and would become foreign to the <term>substance (substantia): the fundamental "stuff" or essence of a thing</term> of the whole, and it would provide the beginning for some external substance. Thus, an external substance would be forged from that part. Just as this is absurd, so you must believe it can in no way happen. 

Since, therefore, God supports himself with infinite and immense power, such that he cannot be torn from himself, nor can he not exist, nor can he "not be able," and "non-existence" does not happen to him; therefore he can neither be divided nor shared. Indeed, if a creature were "cut off" from the substance of God in this way, it would be a portion of the divine substance and separated from the whole of God—which is completely contrary to reason. 

It remains, then, that if God produced all things neither from his own substance, nor from any other external substance <term>co-eternal (coæterna): existing for the same infinite duration as God</term> with him, he must have produced all things from nothing. From <term>non-being (non ente): that which has no existence</term>, from nothing, from that which "is not," he generated and made the universe. For he who truly "Is," and who transcends all being, gave being to that which is not. This certainly cannot be done except by him who, by the infinite efficacy of his power and by the mere nod of his will, does whatever he wishes in heaven and on earth—not, certainly, out of any existing thing, since none preceded it...

<summary>Cosmiel explains the doctrine of creation "ex nihilo," arguing that the universe cannot be made of God's own substance (which is indivisible) nor from pre-existing matter, but must be called into being from nothingness by God's will.</summary>
<keywords>creation ex nihilo, divine substance, indivisibility of God, non-being, cosmology, Theodidactus, Cosmiel</keywords>

### Of Imaginary Space

...existed, therefore, out of nothing, which was to be shown. Furthermore, just as all things were created from nothing by God, so they are balanced and established in nothing. For just as matter is that same thing from which every natural act and form is drawn out—since it is the source of all sensible substance, the prop, foundation, and stabilizing force of all things—so also "nothing" and <term>non-being (non ens): the state of not existing</term> represented to God in the creation of the universe a certain shadowy likeness of matter. For just as matter underlies every natural act, so "nothing" underlies every creature;

<margin>Every creature is established in nothing.</margin>
and every creature is received, placed, and established in nothing. For where all things now are and exist, there was nothing before; and in that nothingness all things were received, out of which they were also made. For they could not have been received into "something," both because there was no "something" or any <term>being (ens): that which has existence</term> in which they could have been placed and situated, and also because if there had been "something," they could not have been received within it, since one being cannot exist and be received within another being. <note>The author is using a philosophical rule that two distinct substances cannot occupy the exact same "being" or essence simultaneously; therefore, the world must occupy the "place" where there was previously nothing.</note> Therefore, everything is in nothing; every fullness is in a <term>void (vacuum): an empty space containing no matter</term>; every being exists within non-being, and is received in it as if in a certain place. For if the divine power were to annihilate the entire "machine of the world" <note>A common Early Modern metaphor describing the universe as a complex, divinely designed mechanism.</note> which He had drawn forth from the beginning, then everywhere nothing else would remain except that which existed before the creation of the world: that is, pure and simple nothingness.

***Theodidactus:*** From this discourse, I gather that the same must be felt regarding that <term>space (spacium): the extent or area</term> which I imagine to be outside the world, as I conceive regarding the space that existed before the world's creation.

***Cosmiel:*** You are completely mistaken if you imagine space to be that, or...

...you should explain what it is "to be" and "to have been" in these terms; for how can you imagine a space for yourself where there is nothing, or how do you say that something "is" or "was" which is nowhere and in no place, and neither can be nor could have been? For all these things involve a manifest contradiction.

***Theodidactus:*** Tell me then, what is that which is outside the world?

***Cosmiel:***
<margin>Imaginary space is explained.</margin>
Once again you fall into the habitual fallacies of human imagination. What this "something" is has no place here, since it is nothing. Therefore, to free you from this error, first be persuaded of this: there is no "nothing" either outside or inside the world. Instead, all of that is a phantom of the human intellect, which thinks that something is there which is not, or thinks that nothing is there when something actually is. <note>Cosmiel is arguing against the idea of a "vacuum" or "void" as a physical thing. He suggests that what humans call "nothing" outside the universe is actually the infinite presence of God.</note> Therefore, establish for yourself and propose to your mind a certain present point, and let your mind soon conceive around it a boundless pouring out of bodily and perfect fullness, actually infinite in every direction of place. This is indeed nothing other than that infinite intellectual sphere whose center is everywhere, but whose circumference is nowhere; <note>original: "sphaera intellectualis, cuius centrum vbique, circumferentia verò nuſquam." This is a famous medieval and Renaissance definition of God's nature.</note> consequently, the mind by no means follows this extension—this <term>actually infinite: a quantity that is truly without end, rather than just potentially growing</term>—nor the whole divine sphere and substance. It neither comprehends it nor closes it within itself. Yet, the mind understands, knows, and perceives it to be infinite, leaping beyond your grasp and surpassing the weak capacity of your mind. For to understand that something is infinite does not, by that very fact, mean that your intelligence encloses and conceives the infinite itself; rather, it is to know and be able to understand that very infinite...

### Of Imaginary Space

...[infi]nite is by no means understood, and it exceeds your capacity without measure or reason; for you do not know God by grasping Him with your mind, nor do you judge Him to be infinite because you embrace Him within the finite little hovel <note>original: "gurgustio," a word meaning a small hut or shack, used here to humble the capacity of the human mind.</note> of your mind; but men know God as infinite because they believe, understand, and know with certain faith that He is inaccessible, inscrutable, and actually immense. 

Therefore, since God is actually infinite, He necessarily also fills every vacuum and empty space (which you conceive as immense and infinite outside the world) with His own substance and presence, banishing from it all "nothingness," or rather every vacuum, 
<margin>There is no "nothing" outside of God.</margin>
void, and non-being; and so it is necessary that neither nothingness, nor void, nor vacuum be left outside of God; for if that nothingness were outside of God, you would be forced to confess that God is by no means infinite; for indeed, the divine substance would be constrained and enclosed by that nothingness, which is impossible; 
<margin>The world does not subsist in nothingness, but in God.</margin>
from which it follows again that the world, received within God, subsists there, and not in nothingness; therefore, when you imagine that <term>imaginary space</term> <note>original: "spacium imaginarium." In 17th-century philosophy, this referred to the infinite void supposed to exist beyond the boundaries of the physical universe.</note> outside the world, you ought to conceive not a nothingness, but the fullness of the divine substance extended into infinity; for He who perfected and created all things, receives, carries, bears, encloses, contains, and preserves those same things in Himself and in His own fullness: for the whole world and all its creatures, compared to God, are nothing other than a point and nothing.

***Theodidactus:*** If therefore God fills all things with His own substance, then you spoke falsely when you said that which we [conceive] outside the world...

...we conceive it to be nothing! **Cosmiel**: You should know that this kind of "space of nothingness" can be considered from two perspectives: either in how it relates to God, or in how it relates to the natural order of beings. 

<margin>Nothingness can be conceived in two ways.</margin>

Viewed in the first way, there is truly no "nothingness" outside the world, because there is nowhere that is not filled with the fullness of the divine substance. But viewed in the second way, we can rightly call it "nothing," since in reality nothing is there except God; and this is how we shall always use the term from now on. But so that you may understand everything more clearly, I will explain these matters to you at greater length.

<margin>A double "aevum" balanced around time,</margin>

Three things must be considered regarding eternity: a double <term>aevum</term> <note>original: "aeuum." In 17th-century philosophy, this refers to a state of duration that has a beginning but no end, often used to describe the "time" of angels or the soul, sitting between human linear time and God's absolute eternity.</note> and the "middle time" between them. This middle time is the measure or duration of the creation and perfection of all things, whether regarding the whole of space or regarding individual and particular things.

<margin>for the time of the creation of all things is the Hexameron</margin>

For the time of the creation of all things—the <term>Hexameron</term> <note>original: "hexameron," the Greek term for the "six days" of creation in Genesis.</note>—is a flow of time. But the time of the completion and consummation of all things through individual and particular beings is the entire duration of this world. 

<margin>of completion and consummation</margin>

Now, God established the physical and visible world within time, and defined for it extremes: a beginning and an end. He balanced it between a double *aevum*. Finally, in the present world, He completes, perfects, and finishes everything that He will contain and preserve in its being throughout the entire future *aevum*. In the first *aevum* (before time), God created nothing; in the future one (after the world ends), He is to create nothing, nor will He grant being to any new substance. Nothing will exist in the future *aevum* which did not have its origin in the present time during the duration of this world.

<margin>Angels from nothing</margin>

He produced the **Angels from nothing** in an instant and at the beginning of time; matter [He produced] after...

### On Imaginary Space

...of this sphere, the same must be said with even better right concerning the whole sphere, in which as many points as exist, so many centers can be established; which, though they may be distant from each other by an infinite space, will always be equidistant from the circumference, which has no end <note>This is a reference to the famous Hermetic definition of God or the infinite: a sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere.</note>. This being so, God could have brought forth worlds separated by an infinite interval from every point of this sphere, if we consider God’s absolute power <note>original: "absolutam Dei potentiam." In Scholastic theology, this refers to what God is capable of doing by His sheer power, regardless of the laws of nature He actually established.</note>; it does not follow, however, that they were actually brought forth, since on the part of matter something irreconcilable with the infinite intervenes. Because matter can never reach the infinite, it seems to constrain and restrict the divine power to the capacity of its own condition; thus, since it cannot be infinite, that which *can* be is what comes to be. Hence, God is so far from having founded infinite worlds that He should rather be judged to have created no other besides this one;

<margin>The world is the maximum contraction.</margin>
Furthermore, since this world contains all things and is the **maximum contraction** <term>contractum maximum: a philosophical concept, notably from Nicholas of Cusa, meaning the greatest possible finite expression of God’s infinite nature</term>, than which a greater cannot be given, other worlds would seem to have been founded in vain. For either those worlds would contain all things, just as this one does, or they would not. If the former, then it would be done in vain through many things what could be done through fewer <note>A variation of "Ockham’s Razor"—the principle that one should not multiply entities unnecessarily.</note>. If the latter, then something would be lacking in those worlds, and they would not contain the full abundance of bodily perfection, which can by no means be said. It remains, therefore, that a single world was founded by God, the Best and Greatest, and that it is the most perfect in every respect; so that just as it is the maximum contraction, it could not have been made better, more perfect, or more absolute; for in this

# CHAPTER X.

## *On the Consummation and Renewal of this Sensible World.*

<margin>The double eternity, together with time, constitutes the whole of eternity.</margin>
**COSMIEL.** I stated above that the **sensible world** <note>The "sensible world" (mundus sensibilis) refers to the physical universe that can be perceived by the human senses, as opposed to the "intelligible world" of ideas or spirits.</note> is balanced between two eternities. The first of these lacks a beginning and ends at the first instant of the creation of all things; the latter has a beginning but lacks an end, and its start is to be taken from the beginning of the **renewal of all things**—that is, after the final sentence of the eternal Judge has been pronounced. Thus, the span of time between both eternities consists only of a beginning and an end, insofar as the world is considered in its unstable, successive flow, subject to corruptions and generations. The double **eternity** <term>ævum: in Scholastic philosophy, this often refers to "eviternity," a mode of duration for beings like angels who have a beginning but no end, distinct from the absolute eternity of God</term> is joined by time, just as two lines extending to infinity in both directions might be joined by a single point. For just as there is no proportion between a point and a line, so there is no proportion between time—however long it may last—and eternity, which the two lines joined by the point of time represent.

**Theodidactus:** Why did God, the Best, wish to insert a flowing and fleeting time into eternity?

**Cosmiel:** The purpose of God, the Best and Greatest, in the production of the world was, first, that in time [His] glory...

# CHAPTER XI.

->*The purpose for which God created the World, and concerning the Incarnation of Christ, and the Faith of the Church through which God willed to save men.*<-

<margin>A doubt as to whether the world was created for the sake of man alone.</margin>
**THEODIDACTUS.** As I weigh a little more deeply the immense mass of the World joined to such a diversity of spheres, no few doubts occur which strike my mind: why God, the Greatest and Best, created such a machine <term>machine: a common Baroque metaphor (the *machina mundi*) describing the universe as a complex, divinely engineered mechanism</term>; whether for man alone? # On the Purpose of the Creation of the World.

<margin>A comparison of the creation of the world with the Incarnation of the Word.</margin>
***Cosmiel:*** Theodidactus, which do you think is greater: that this world was produced by God out of nothing, or that God was made man for the sake of man—choosing to inhabit this earthly speck and wishing to show man the way to eternal salvation through the performance of stupendous works? ***Theodidactus:*** I judge the Incarnation of the Son of God to be a work many leagues <note>original: "parasangis." # On the End of the Creation of the World

<sig>Fff 2</sig>

<margin>
Human nature in Christ is the maximum contracted; it could not subsist except in the Word <note>The "Word" (Latin: *Verbum*) refers to the second person of the Trinity, the eternal Son of God.</note>.
</margin>

...Therefore, such a being could neither exist on its own, nor could it be the Absolute Maximum (who is God). It necessarily follows that such a <term>maximum contracted</term> <note>original: "maximum contractum." A term for the highest possible state of a created, limited thing.</note>, when united to the <term>Absolute Maximum</term> <note>God, the infinite and unconditioned source of all reality.</note>, would be simultaneously God and creature. It could not exist except within the Absolute Maximum. Since there is only one Absolute Maximum—from whom the "maximum contracted" receives its greatness—if the Maximum Power were to unite such a being to itself in such a way that both natures remained preserved while reaching the highest possible state of union, it is certain that such a union would exceed all limits of the human intellect. 

Such was human nature. Elevated above all God’s other works through this union, it folds together both intellectual and sensible nature, binding them within itself by a link; for this reason, it is rightly called a <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "microcosmus," meaning "little world." This is the ancient and medieval idea that a human being is a miniature map or reflection of the entire universe.</note>. Because this human nature was taken up into union with the Absolute Maximum, it exists as the perfection of all things in the universe, whether taken as a whole or individually. In this humanity, all things reach their highest degree. Thus, Christ is so much a man that he is God, and so much God that he is man. He is the perfection of the universe, holding primacy over all things. In him, the highest, the lowest, and the middle things are united to the Absolute Maximum and coincide in such a way that he himself is the perfection of all. 

All finite, "contracted" things find their rest in him as their own perfection. He is the measure of man, of Angels, and of every individual thing, because he is the universal contracted entity of all universals. Through him, all things look toward the beginning and the end of their finite existence. Through him, who is the <term>maximum contracted</term> proceeding from the Absolute Maximum, all things come into their finite being, and through him as the mediator, they return to the Absolute.

...and is almost the common opinion of the Holy Fathers <note>original: "SS. PP." (Sanctorum Patrum), referring to the authoritative early Christian theologians.</note>; this union is not indeed a physical and natural one, by which one thing is forged from two mutually incomplete parts, so that each part might then be completed and perfected through the bond of their mutual union. Instead, it is purely "numerical" <note>In scholastic philosophy, a "numerical" union refers to two things becoming one in number/identity rather than mixing their physical substances.</note> and intrinsic—as the Theologians say—supernatural, and existing through a certain ineffable <note>Too great or sacred to be expressed in words.</note> way. In this way, according to the testimony of Saint Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent philosopher and theologian of the Catholic Church.</note>, a single thing is constituted in itself from two parts, one of which is imperfect and incomplete, and capable of being completed and perfected by the other. The other part, however, is essentially and ultimately complete, and by no means capable of being completed or perfected by the other extreme; such is the <term>Divine Word</term> <note>original: "Verbum diuinum." The second person of the Trinity, the eternal Son of God.</note>. Therefore, although the <term>hypostatic union</term> <note>The union of Christ's humanity and divinity in one individual existence.</note> unites the <term>Word</term> to humanity, and humanity to the <term>Word</term>, it does not affect both of these extremes in the same way. For it perfects and completes the humanity, serving as the means by which it is done, and therefore it changes the humanity intrinsically by such a proper <term>change</term> <note>original: "immutatio." A technical term for a transition from one state to another.</note>. But the <term>Divine Word</term> is neither completed nor perfected in any way, and accordingly it is not changed intrinsically, because the union neither adds to it nor takes away from it any <term>perfection</term> <note>In this context, "perfection" refers to a quality or attribute that completes a thing's nature.</note>—either of which would be required for the concept of an intrinsic change. Therefore, the <term>Divine Word</term> is united to humanity as if actively, by communicating its own perfection to it; humanity, however, is united to the <term>Word</term> purely passively, receiving and conferring no perfection. Thus, the mode of the <term>hypostatic union</term> is indeed a true composition of the <term>Word</term> and humanity, yet it is not a true change of both, but of humanity alone—

<margin>Heretics do not possess supernatural faith.</margin>
**Theodidactus:** Heretics believe that all things have been revealed in the Holy Scriptures, and they follow this as the sole interpreter of the divine will and an infallible rule; since they believe in the revealing divine authority, should they not therefore be judged to have true faith? 

**Cosmiel:** It is true that they read the Holy Scriptures with the greatest zeal and interpret them by their own intellect; but in doing this, what else are they doing than you, when you explain the more difficult passages of **Aristotle** or **Plato** using your own mind? Just as you, in explaining those authors, produce no act of faith, so too it is with them. Therefore, as long as heretics explain **Holy Scripture** by the power of their own intellect <note>original: "proprij ingenij vi"; referring to the use of human reason alone without the guidance of Church tradition.</note> and believe it must be understood in that way, they produce no act of divine faith, but an act of pure and simple opinion.

<margin>Why heretics are so greatly perplexed.</margin>
And from this comes such great confusion among heretics, and such instability in asserting matters of faith; while one person thinks the passages of Holy Scripture should be understood one way and another person another way, they are pulled apart into different directions. Wonderfully doubtful, perplexed, and confused, they give birth to countless monsters—not of faith, but of opinions. Experience teaches this among the followers of the teachings of **Calvin** <note>John Calvin (1509–1564), a principal figure in the development of the system of Christian theology later called Calvinism.</note> and **Luther**; <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the German priest who was a seminal figure in the Protestant Reformation.</note> among them, there are as many disparate views on matters of faith as there are cities; as many religions as there are families; finally, one can see as many disagreements of different opinions as there are heads. And do you think these people have true faith? Oh, how far you wander from the truth!

<margin>The conditions of true faith.</margin>
Faith, to be true, must be one, holy, **Catholic**, and in conformity with the **Church**, which is the foundation of truth, the pillar of rectitude, and the infallible rule of things to be believed; from which whoever [departs] even in the smallest <note>The sentence ends abruptly here due to the page break; the catchword "nimo" suggests the next word is "animo" or "minimo," continuing the thought that even a small mental departure from Church teaching disqualifies one from true faith.</note>

For wisdom, which is true faith, does not enter into a malevolent soul subject to sins. This is also for me a most brilliant argument for an unjust faith: that no such sects endure for a long time, but with time, completely crushing themselves by their own ruin, they are extinguished. Added to these is a supreme inconstancy, by which, not knowing how to stand firm, they go now into this sect, now into that, until at last they degenerate into open <term>atheism</term>, destitute of all faith. 

All these things cease in the Catholic Church, whose faith is founded not on man, but on Christ the Son of God. It is so far from ever having turned aside that it has instead daily received greater growth, propagated throughout the whole world, <margin>The constancy of the Catholic Church.</margin> where inconstancy does not rule, but supreme uniformity, rectitude, and justice. Where occurring doubts are decided not by a private teacher, but by the visible head of the Church, the Supreme Pontiff, the <term>Vicar of Christ</term><note>original: "Vicarius Christi"; a title for the Pope signifying his role as the earthly representative of Christ.</note> on earth and successor of Peter, by the promise made by Christ and the invisible assistance of the Holy Spirit. # CHAPTER XII

->*Why GOD, though He created so much for the sake of man, allows so few to attain eternal salvation, and concerning the hidden judgments of God.*<-

<margin>The hidden judgments of God.</margin> **T**HEODIDACTUS. While I explore the magnitude of the world a little more deeply, while I weigh more precisely that innumerable multitude of celestial bodies, while I consider this earthly globe—a great part of which is still unknown—I remain in doubt. ### On the fewness of those to be saved.
<sig>Iii 2</sig>

Having gazed upon the condition of his own weakness, man should serve God with fear and trembling and cling to Him more closely through faith; through hope he should long more ardently for the delights of divine fruition <note>The theological term for the soul's ultimate happiness and "enjoyment" of God in heaven.</note>; and through charity <note>original: "charitatem"; referring here to the virtue of divine love.</note> finally be united to Him more perfectly, until, released from the weight of the fleshy burden, he might at last enjoy Him eternally. For there, they shall behold all things in the light of life; there they shall contemplate all the reasons for divine works, the structure and fabric of the world, and the causes of everything contained within it, perfectly, with an ineffable and everlasting joy. For there, the goodness and wisdom of God—the root and principle of all divine works—shall be perfectly known; and indeed, God's goodness grants things their essence, while His wisdom confers their laws. 

From the highest and inscrutable abyss of divine wisdom, therefore, the world proceeded under such a specific mass of magnitude, and under such a number of stars and celestial bodies—neither greater nor smaller than they are. He assigned separate distances to each, and different ratios of influences <term>influxuum</term><note>A technical term in Renaissance cosmology referring to the spiritual or physical "flow" of power from the stars to the earth.</note> and virtues, which no one but He alone knows, though they are to be manifested in their proper place in the Word of Life. 

<margin>Why God has permitted such great evils.</margin>
From this storehouse of infinite wisdom proceeded that which men are so accustomed to wonder at: why a yoke of such unequal condition has pressed upon the human race—why He willed one to be weighed down by poverty, and another exalted with glory and riches; this one miserable through the perpetual vexation of diseases, that one flourishing in strength and vigor; this one cast down by the arrows of unfair fortune, and another prospering with the happy success of all things.

# CONCLUSION
# OF THE WORK

## With the Author's Declaration <note>original: "protestatione" — in this context, a formal public statement or clarification of intent to ensure the work is not misunderstood by religious authorities.</note>.

**Y**OU HAVE here, Kind Reader, in this *Ecstatic Journey*, my opinion regarding the World and the structure and composition of the celestial bodies, pointed out under the cover and veil of a fictional rapture. I would ask this one thing of you: that you do not interpret the perhaps somewhat bold title <note>original: "prænotationem" — referring to the title "Ecstatic Journey," which might imply a literal supernatural claim.</note> of this work in a negative way; but rather, I would have you be persuaded that it was done for no other purpose than to instill the teaching of an unusual subject into the mind of the reader with a more pleasant and agreeable reasoning. Thus, just as the mind is made more attentive to each question and answer proposed back and forth, it might become more eager for what follows. I hoped to achieve this in no better way than by following the spirit of the poets and dramatists, presenting these narrations concerning the vast dwellings of the world through the introduced characters of **Cosmiel** and **Theodidactus** <gloss>Cosmiel is the angelic guide (whose name implies "Order of God"); Theodidactus is the student (meaning "Taught by God"), representing Kircher himself.</gloss>, and showing them as explored through simulated raptures into the inner recesses of a higher nature. In this way, as the saying goes, I might provoke inspiration with inspiration <note>original: "Enthusiasmo enthusiasmum prouocarem" — Kircher is using "enthusiasm" in its Greek sense of divine possession or intense poetic inspiration to engage the reader's imagination.</note>; if, moreover, perhaps some descriptions...

<summary>Athanasius Kircher explains that the fictional narrative of an angelic journey was a literary device intended to make complex astronomical theories more engaging and accessible to the reader.</summary>

# Conclusion.

...expressed more hyperbolically <note>original Greek: ὑπερβολικωτέρως (*hyperbolikōterōs*)</note>, should the Reader find them; I would wish him to ascribe it to the heat of a restless intellect playing in the manner of Poets, for so the design of the subject proposed to us required.
->*While my soaring mind does not permit me to be my own master*<-
Indeed, I judged this style of writing to be more effective for seizing the reader's mind and fixing it upon the proposed matters for weighing with deeper reasoning. But as far as opinions on physical truths are concerned, let no one think me possessed of such shameless audacity or such a stubborn mind that I would attempt to arrogantly <note>original Greek: ὑπερηφάνως (*hyperēphanōs*)</note> thrust forward the positions asserted in this work as if they were—as the saying goes—a rule of Gospel truth <note>Kircher is carefully distinguishing his scientific speculations from Church dogma to avoid conflict with religious authorities.</note>, established by an irrefragable weight of arguments. Far be such confidence from a religious heart; for I have never permitted a similar stain of self-love <note>original Greek: φιλαυτίας (*philautias*), referring here to vanity or intellectual conceit</note> to settle in my mind. I know that saying of the Wise Man: *All things are difficult, and they cannot be explained in speech* <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:8.</note>; I know that however much anyone may have progressed in investigating the paths of divine Wisdom, he will always find himself as much further from the target of truth as he has drawn near to it; and he will find that as many more things remain for him to learn as the things he already knows. Wherefore, just as there are a thousand human perceptions and a thousand differences of minds, so I leave to each person the freest will and judgment to feel whatever they wish concerning this work. This only I say: he who knows the secrets of the analogical art <term>analogical art: the method of understanding celestial or spiritual realities by comparing them to known physical or mathematical principles</term> will most truly discover that this is, by the bounty of the divine gift, like a certain key for the weakness of the human intellect...

## Conclusion.

Just like the earth, the Stars <note>original: *Astra*. In 17th-century cosmology, this term often referred generally to any celestial body, including planets.</note> subsist by their own centers; therefore, the parts of each globe or Star will, by a natural appetite, partly flow together toward the center proper to each, and partly flow away from it. If this is so, then just as there is a downward movement of solid parts toward their center, so too is there an outward expulsion of light parts exhaled from that same center; therefore, each Star consists of its own atmosphere. If they have atmospheres, then moisture cannot be absent from them; if there is moisture, then there is also solid matter, which contains the moisture as if in a vessel. 

But these things cannot be preserved without heat dissolving the moisture, nor can this happen without the assistance of intervening air. Therefore, it is necessary that each and every Star be composed of the four elements <note>The classic elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note>, each endowed with a peculiar privilege according to the nature of the position they hold. 

If this is so, then from these elements—just as from all composite things—there will result an emanation of diverse properties, forms, and influences, accompanied by a perpetual cycle of alterations. It follows by necessity that continuous generation and corruption <note>original: *generatio & corruptio*. A standard Aristotelian phrase referring to the process of things being born/formed and then breaking down/decaying.</note> must result. 

The Stars are therefore subject to decay, because they are subject to alterations; they are subject to alterations because they are mixtures; they are mixtures because they are composed of elements, possessing solid, moist, airy, and fiery or hot qualities. If they are composed of elements, then they have an atmosphere agitated by the flow of heavy and light things; therefore they consist of their own centers of gravity; therefore it is impossible for them to be tied to solid spheres <note>Kircher is arguing against the traditional Aristotelian model where planets were thought to be embedded in hard, transparent "crystalline spheres" like gems in a ring.</note>. Therefore, they move in a liquid; therefore the heaven is liquid <term>liquidum|fluid, non-solid, or yielding</term> and everywhere permeable, which was the point to be demonstrated. You see, therefore, that with the liquid heaven established, all things said from

## Conclusion.

St. Bruno, founder of the Carthusians <note>Saint Bruno of Cologne (c. 1030–1101), the founder of the Carthusian Order.</note>, in his commentaries on Psalm 148: *Praise him Sun and Moon, praise him all stars and light, because he spoke and they were made* <note>original Latin: "Laudate eum Sol & Luna, laudate eum omnes ſtellæ & lumen, quia ipſe dixit & facta ſunt"</note>; namely, the **four elements** <term>four elements</term><note>In classical and medieval science, these were Earth, Water, Air, and Fire, the building blocks of all matter.</note> which were the matter of all these things; He Himself commanded and all these were created—that is, formed from these four elements.

Anselm, Bishop of Canterbury <note>Saint Anselm (c. 1033–1109), a hugely influential medieval philosopher and theologian.</note>, *On the Image of the World*, book 1, chapter 23: *The Sun is called "Sol" because it shines above all things, spherical in form, and fiery in nature. And the body of the Moon is globular, fiery in nature, but mixed with water.* And in chapter 20 regarding the stars: *Furthermore, all stars are round and fiery, the arrangement of which is known to God alone.*

Fabrizio Paolucci, Bishop of Forlì <note>An Italian bishop and theologian (1582–1625).</note>, in his *Commentary on Genesis*: *We cannot ignore how clearly Scripture speaks that the waters placed above the firmament <note>In the Book of Genesis, the "firmament" or sky is described as separating waters below (oceans) from waters above.</note> were true and elementary waters, just as those which remained below the firmament. Therefore, those are true and elementary waters, not changed into anything else.* And regarding the Second Epistle of St. Peter, chapter 3, he says: *The heavens pass away with a great rush.* Whether this refers to all the heavens, or only the airy space, is a great difficulty; but we concede that it means all of them, since all the heavens were formed from the primary matter from which the four elements were compacted.

Ludovico Lacerda of the Society of Jesus <note>A Spanish Jesuit scholar (1560–1640) known for his extensive literary and theological commentaries.</note>, in his *Notebooks*: *Many of the Holy Fathers strive to prove from Scripture—not from the opinion of Plato—that the heavens are **corruptible** <term>corruptible</term><note>Meaning subject to physical change, decay, or dissolution, a radical idea that challenged the Aristotelian belief that the stars were eternal and unchanging.</note>. Ambrose, in the first book of the Hexameron, chapter 6, mocks those who say with Aristotle...*

*That heaven is a fifth essence, and not counted among the elements. Another opinion holds that the Heavens are incorruptible. What should I say in the face of such variety? I certainly consider the former opinion <note>referring to the argument on the previous page that the heavens are composed of the four basic elements</note> to be the most true, and that all the Heavens are corruptible. Why philosophers have insisted with such great effort on proving the incorruptibility of the Heavens, I have long wondered; and indeed, as far as I can discern, no other thing motivates them except to keep Aristotle <note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose theories dominated science for centuries, teaching that the heavens were perfect and unchanging.</note> safe and intact. It is a remarkable praise indeed to prefer him to so many heavenly men. I have no doubt that he erred, as did as many as defend his opinion.*

Marin Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648) was a French priest and mathematician often called the "post-box of Europe" because of his vast correspondence with scientists like Descartes and Galileo.</note> of the Order of Minims <term>Order of Minims</term><note>A Roman Catholic religious order founded by St. Francis of Paola.</note>, in his *Commentary on Genesis*, page 843: *That all the Heavens, in which the Stars are seen to move, are fluid like the air; this opinion is not beset by as many inconveniences as the opposing one, and is the easiest of all. Look for him in the cited place, where he proves his opinion with eight reasons: from optical necessity, from the irregular motion of comets, from the production of new stars, and from the horned Moon <note>The crescent moon as seen through early telescopes.</note> which is unequal, rough, and covered everywhere with pits and valleys, from Sunspots, and from the Jovian and Saturnian stars <note>The moons of Jupiter and the unusual appearances of Saturn (its rings), which were newly discovered at this time.</note>, where he says the stars are necessarily subject to birth, decay, and change; since these things are treated more extensively than can be placed here, I refer the reader to the cited place.*

# Conclusion.

From *General Matters*, Volume 2, Question 34, page 160: *Finally, therefore, it must be admitted that sunspots are truly and really in the Sun, because to those looking at the Sun through a tube <note>original: "tubum"—a common 17th-century term for the recently invented telescope</note>, a certain intense sparkling and a kind of boiling of the Sun is found in its entire circumference, and these same things are found in the spots dispersed throughout the whole middle of the Sun. Therefore, these spots are really in the Sun, and are agitated along with it. But as to how this happens, and what the nature of these spots finally is, two ways occur: the first is, if it be said that the Sun is not a certain solid body, but a fluid contained in its place as if in a vessel, and is agitated within itself like boiling metal, and in it certain opaque and dark parts are found, etc.*

Petrus Hurtadus de Mendoza <note>Pedro Hurtado de Mendoza (1578–1641) was a prominent Spanish Jesuit philosopher known for bridging medieval scholasticism and early modern science.</note> of the Society of Jesus, Book 1, *On the Universe*: That Aristotle asserted the Heaven was not made <note>referring to the ancient Greek idea that the universe had no beginning</note> is such a famous insanity that it does not need a refutation; and much less does his claim that God, by fatal necessity, moves the heaven in such a way that it cannot cease from motion. For so he says in text 134 of *On the Heavens* <note>Aristotle's "De Caelo," the foundational text for ancient and medieval astronomy</note>: *“Moreover, it is also to be considered thus: that it is impossible either for something made at some time to endure as incorruptible, or for what is ungenerated and always previously existing to be corrupted.”* Therefore, from here he [Aristotle] infers that the heaven is neither generable nor corruptible; for everything, he says, that begins to be, at some time ceases to be; for what is such is made of matter, and is therefore corruptible; and what is corruptible will at some time be corrupted. Whence he [Hurtado] rightly concludes that if Aristotle asserted by hypothesis that the heaven began in time, he also asserted that it would naturally cease and be corrupted at some time.

Ismaël Boulliau <note>Ismaël Boulliau (1605–1694) was a prominent French mathematician and astronomer, best known for his "Astronomia Philolaica," which was among the first to suggest that the force of gravity follows an inverse-square law.</note>, Parisian Royal Mathematician, Part 4 of *Philolaic Astronomy*: *I can scarcely understand why the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who generally believed that the heavens were made of a solid, unchanging fifth element called "ether."</note> attributed such solid matter to the heavens. For how, I ask, could the lunar body and the sphere in which it is moved be fashioned from the same matter? The body of the Moon is solid and dark, and it blocks our sight; therefore, its sphere must be as well. Shortly after, if they respond that the lunar body consists of a denser part of the sphere, this weapon must be turned back against them; for since, in their opinion, the spheres and the stars fixed within them are simple and homogeneous bodies, consisting of similar parts: If, therefore, both the Moon and its sphere consist of the same matter, the body of the Moon will be simple, and the matter of its sphere homogeneous; it will therefore not be possible for it to be affected by contrary forms at the same time—namely, for the Moon to be affected by opacity, and the sphere by transparency. Since the Moon is opaque and the sphere in which it is carried is transparent, it is necessary that such bodies be heterogeneous <note>made of different substances</note>; thus Aristotle argued incorrectly when he made heterogeneous things homogeneous, and gathered equals and likes from things that are different and dissimilar. Furthermore, how can bodies that rest upon different centers be of the same matter? For homogeneous things, when united together, look toward a single center, etc.*

Scheiner, *Rosa Ursina* <note>Christoph Scheiner (1573–1650) was a Jesuit astronomer and rival to Galileo; his "Rosa Ursina" is a massive treatise on sunspots and solar physics.</note>, page 740: This author, in his massive work *Rosa Ursina*, does nothing other than destroy the solidity and incorruptibility of the heavens; he asserts the atmospheres of the stars and their motions around their own centers. Therefore, I refer the reader to the cited work.

## Conclusion.

Johannes Hevelius <note>Johannes Hevelius (1611–1687) was a wealthy brewer and astronomer from Danzig (Gdańsk) who built a world-class observatory and produced the first detailed maps of the Moon.</note> in *Selenographia* <note>original: "Stelenographia"—the 1647 masterpiece that founded the science of lunar description.</note> folio 148.

> *First, it is asked what the roughness and flatness of the Moon really is in truth—that is, from what matter it consists, and to what material it can most rightly be compared. I respond: the tuberous and uneven part of the Moon, which is brighter than the others, can be compared to no other earthly things known to us more suitably than to the Earth itself and its continents; for it receives into itself almost all the qualities of the Earth. It is not, however, that anyone should therefore think the Moon is composed of such sand, mud, and stone as this earth of ours, since it could perhaps consist of another matter altogether different from our imagination and in a way still incomprehensible to us. I boldly affirm all this: these protruding, rougher, and brighter parts can be compared to nothing here on earth better than to the continent; for which reason we shall hereafter call this "land." Regarding the lower, flatter places of the Moon—those large spots that always offer themselves to us as darker than the mountainous places—they are no less appropriately likened to our oceans, seas, lakes, ponds, and marshes; for these also have their own windings, bays, and promontories. I by no means assert, however, that these lunar waters are identical to ours, but only that we have nothing here on earth more similar with which we might compare them, due to the great affinity between the two. I conclude, therefore, that the clearly illuminated surface is land, but the darker spots are waters, just as Kepler <note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), the German astronomer who formulated the laws of planetary motion.</note> also concedes in his* Dissertation with the Starry Messenger <note>original: "dissertat: cum nuncio sidereo"—Kepler's 1610 open letter supporting Galileo’s telescope discoveries.</note> *of Galileo.*

Francesco Patrizi of Italy <note>original: "Franciscus Patricius Italus"—Patrizi (1529–1597) was a Venetian philosopher whose work *Nova de Universis Philosophia* challenged Aristotle’s grip on science.</note>, Book 20 of *Pancosmia* <note>The section of Patrizi's work dealing with the physical nature of the entire universe.</note>.

Therefore, it might not be far from the truth that the globe of the Moon is another globe of earth, formed into a sphere together with all its water—an ethereal globe, in fact, just as our globe is a <term>material one <note>original: "hylæus," a term derived from the Greek "hyle," meaning matter or substance.</note></term>. And that part of the Moon which shines with the light of the Sun is that other "ethereal water." By its own gravity, this water does not fall toward us, for this center <note>referring to Earth</note> is not the Moon’s center; rather, that water tends toward the Moon's center in the same way our water tends toward our own center. The same applies to the other parts of the lunar earth, just like the parts of our own earth. What would be so strange, then, if there were plains, mountains, and valleys there, just as on our earth?

And a little later: Indeed, it is certain that all our seas are moved in various ways according to the various appearances of the Moon; the flow and ebb of the seas, as well as other tides and fluids, are most clearly drawn and withdrawn by the light of the Moon. These things would not happen at all unless a great <term>sympathy <note>In 17th-century science, "sympathy" referred to a natural attraction or shared relationship between two physical bodies, such as the Moon and the Earth's tides.</note></term> existed between that body and our own. This sympathy exists only because of a great agreement in both forces and actions, and this agreement consists only in a similarity of essence. Thus says Hevelius.

# Conclusion.

*...our <term>watery globe</term> <note>original: "aqueus noster globus"; referring to the Earth as seen from space.</note>, seen from the Moon, would appear less illuminated in its watery parts and more in its land parts. Just as happens in the <term>lunar phases</term> <note>original: "phasibus lunaribus"</note>, from which it is argued that the moist parts of the Moon have <term>influences</term> <note>original: "influentijs"; in 17th-century science, "influences" were physical or astrological flows from celestial bodies that affected Earthly matter.</note>; since these greatly moisten—as is evident in plants and animals being perceptibly more moist at the time of the full moon—it is argued that the source is moist. This source, excited by the light and heat of the Sun’s rays at the full moon, communicates itself more abundantly to the earth than when the Moon is less full.*

*Also concerning the stars, on page 612: It is certain that all planets are always directly viewed by the Sun, since they are above the vertex of the dark cone <note>A reference to the shadow cast by a planet; an eclipse occurs when another body enters this "cone of shadow."</note> projected by the terrestrial globe and other planets (except perhaps for Jupiter and Saturn, which are the highest). However, it has never been observed that any of the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>original: "fixarum"; the stars that do not move relative to one another, as opposed to the "wandering" planets.</note> are eclipsed by these planets. Thus, nothing could be lacking in this model except for the excessive distance from the Sun. Because many other scholars suppose this distance, they maintain that those stars shine with their own light and are, as it were, other fiery Suns. For if they shine by their own power, then for the same reasons we brought forward for the fiery Sun, they themselves must properly be called fiery.*

*Also concerning the center of the Moon and the other stars, on page 611: Nor is there a danger that lunar parts, or the whole Moon, might fall to the earth, if its matter is compatible with ours and its form is not dissimilar. For all parts are inclined toward the center of the globe of which they are parts, for the same reasons that this occurs on earth. Even if the Earth had been placed in another part of the <term>ether</term> <note>original: "ætheris"; the substance believed to fill the upper regions of space.</note>, it would have remained fixed there in the same way; for the whole does not tend toward an imaginary center of the universe, but the parts only strive toward the whole.* <note>This is a significant early modern insight into gravity: that objects fall toward the center of their own planet rather than a single fixed point in the center of the universe.</note>

The Solar Eclipse of January 26, in the year 1656, observed with the greatest zeal and sagacious industry by the Most Illustrious and Reverend Lord Juan Caramuel, with the help of Eustachio Divini <note>Eustachio Divini (1610–1685) was a renowned Italian optical instrument maker and astronomer, famous for his high-quality telescopes.</note>, and printed at Rome, number 7.

*Furthermore, we saw that the edge of the Sun was wavy and stormy, and we began to doubt whether it might be liquid. For if the solar body were solid, we would not perceive from Earth such great tempests of bubbling shadows and splendors. Here I have allowed everyone to abound in their own opinion <note>original: "in suo sensu abundare"; a common Latin expression for allowing individual interpretation.</note>, for the Sun is far removed from us, and in such a sublime and subtle matter, the opinions of illustrious men vary. Among these, the opinion prevails which asserts that the spheres of the planets are <term>pervious</term> <note>original: "pervias"; meaning they are not solid crystal shells but can be passed through.</note> and that in the wandering globes <note>The "wandering globes" refer to the planets.</note> two materials are found: one solid and similar to earth, the other liquid and analogous to water. And a little later, when at the same time a greater marvel of the Sun seemed to revolve from A through FCE <note>These letters likely referred to a diagram in the original printed report.</note> against the <term>succession of the signs</term> <note>original: "contra signorum successionem"; this refers to movement in the opposite direction of the zodiac signs, or retrograde motion.</note> with the highest velocity—and why is that, I ask? Does the Sun move around its own center very rapidly? And if it moves, does it move from East to West against the succession of the signs? If one distrusts the eyes, all is safe; but because the senses guide us and we are bound to believe them as long as it is not clear that they err, I therefore affirm that the Sun, insofar as it is solid, turns upon its axes in a <term>monthly space</term> <note>original: "menstruo spacio"; Caramuel is noting that the Sun completes a rotation roughly once a month, as evidenced by the movement of sunspots.</note> (as the <term>sunspots</term> <note>original: "maculae"</note> require); but insofar as it is liquid, it flows in various directions, wherever either the gravity of the matter or the force of the solar winds drives the waves, etc.*

Juan Eusebio Nieremberg <note>A Spanish Jesuit polymath and author (1595–1658) known for his works on natural history and mystical theology.</note>, *Natural History*, Book 2, Chapter 13: "On the Corruptibility of the Heaven." O how ridiculous we are, when we know by our faith that the heavens are to be <term>destroyed</term> <note>original: "corrumpendos"; in 17th-century theological physics, "corruption" referred to the physical decay or the eventual transformation of the material universe at the end of time.</note>.

<summary>This page records Juan Caramuel’s 1656 observation of a solar eclipse, arguing that the Sun's "stormy" appearance suggests it is composed of both solid and liquid matter. It concludes with a theological reflection from Nieremberg on the eventual decay or transformation of the heavens.</summary>
<keywords>Solar Eclipse 1656, Juan Caramuel, Eustachio Divini, sunspots, solar rotation, fluid Sun, Juan Eusebio Nieremberg, corruptibility of the heavens</keywords>

<page-num>459</page-num>
->**Conclusion.**<-

...if we still make them <term>perishable</term> <note>original: "corruptibiles"; in 17th-century natural philosophy, this refers to the ability of a substance to change, decay, or be transformed, contrasting with the Aristotelian view that the heavens were "incorruptible" and eternal.</note>; many philosophers, thinking they would never be destroyed, nevertheless called them perishable. God does nothing in vain; why would He build incorruptible spheres if He intended to destroy them? Why do you wonder that the heavens are perishable and yet not destroyed, though one might indeed wonder that they were made for this purpose? This is proposed to the holy man Job among the wonders of God: *Perhaps you, like Him, built the heavens, which are most solid as if cast from bronze.* <note>A reference to Job 37:18. The author is navigating the paradox of the heavens being "subtle" (thin) yet "firm."</note> Truly this is worth wondering at: that the heavens, being most subtle, contain the whole ether, secure, as if they were most solid and made of bronze. God can make firm what is thin; hence the name <term>firmament</term> was given to the heavens, because they were made firm by the word and power of God. They are not firm of themselves, but *made firm* [by Him]; therefore Isaiah joins the likeness of physical smoke with firmness: *The heavens,* he says, *have been made firm like smoke.* <note>A reference to Isaiah 51:6. The Latin "firmatum est" implies being strengthened or solidified by an external force.</note>

And in the same place, chapter 11. I shall transcribe what Johann Baptist Cysat <note>Johann Baptist Cysat (1587–1657) was a Swiss Jesuit mathematician and astronomer and a pioneer in using the telescope for celestial observation.</note>, an astronomer of diligent industry and judgment, sent to me not long ago in a letter from Barcelona in the year 1628. He informs me thus: "And indeed, in the recent solar eclipse, which occurred on the very day of Christ's birth <note>Christmas Day, 1628.</note>, I clearly observed something in the Moon as it was positioned beneath the Sun, which strongly proves the very same thing that comets and <term>sunspots</term> <note>original: "maculæ solares"; the discovery of sunspots by Galileo and others challenged the idea of celestial perfection.</note> also suggest. Namely, that the heavens are not exempt from the thinness and variations of the air. For I noticed that around the Moon there is a certain **vaporous sphere** or orb, not unlike the one around the Earth. And just as vapors and exhalations breathe out from the Earth into a certain sphere, so too they do from the Moon. If Your Reverence had been with me and had looked at the Moon beneath the Sun, I would have demonstrated to Your Reverence both by reason and to the eyes..."

<summary>The author argues that the heavens are "perishable" and made firm only by God's power, citing biblical passages and a 1628 letter from astronomer Johann Baptist Cysat describing a lunar atmosphere.</summary>
<keywords>perishability, firmament, Job, Isaiah, Johann Baptist Cysat, solar eclipse, lunar atmosphere, sunspots, celestial physics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the physical nature of the heavens. <page-num>460</page-num>
->**On the Ecstatic Journey**<-
<meta>Catchword: At-</meta>

...heaven, as I say, is something I now certainly know. Therefore, the heavens do not consist of an unchanging density; rather, a very thin, very pure, and yielding substance was necessary for the forward and outward movement, and for such great ascent and descent of the <term>wandering stars</term> <note>original: "stellarum errantium"; this is the literal translation of the Greek word "planētēs," from which we get "planets."</note>. For <term>epicycles</term> <note>In the older Ptolemaic system, these were small circular orbits whose centers moved around the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent), used to explain why planets sometimes appear to move backward.</note> are insufficient and impossible. Philosophy also rejects excavated channels <note>A reference to the theory that planets move through "grooves" or "tracks" in the celestial spheres.</note> no less than it loathes a vacuum, which is contrary to nature. Therefore, the movements of the stars could not be carried out except in a permeable space suitable for dispersing their paths. I marvel at how consistent the truth is with itself, and how **Holy Scripture** agrees with reason and true philosophy.

> Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book 6, Chapter 6. The ancients should be heard with an excuse. Nothing is finished while it is just beginning; and not only in this matter—the greatest and most intricate of all (namely **Astronomical discipline**), in which even when much has been achieved, every age will still find something to do—but in every other business, the beginnings have always been far from perfect. Everything was new to those first attempting it; later these same things were refined, and if anything has been discovered, it must nonetheless be credited to them. It was an act of great spirit to move aside the hiding places of nature, and not being content with its outward appearance, to look within and descend into the secrets of the Gods. He who hoped it could be found contributed most to the discovery.

> Ibidem <note>Latin for "in the same place."</note> Book 7, Chapter 31. The people of a coming age will know many things unknown to us; many things are reserved for future centuries when the memory of us has faded. The world is a tiny thing unless it contains something for the whole world to seek within it.

<summary>Kircher argues that the heavens are made of a thin, fluid substance rather than solid spheres, allowing planets to move freely without the need for complex epicycles. He supports this by citing Seneca on the progressive nature of scientific discovery and the vastness of nature's secrets.</summary>
<keywords>celestial fluid, epicycles, planetary motion, Seneca, history of astronomy, fluid heavens, scientific progress</keywords>

# Conclusion.

And these authorities will suffice to establish our opinion. Countless others could have been added, but lest this little work exceed its proper bounds of size, I have thought it best to rest content with these few among many. 

Whoever desires these matters to be treated at greater length, I advise them to consult the works of the authors contained in the following table; nor should the reader be disturbed if they find some <term>unconventional ideas</term> <note>original: "παράδοξα" (paradoxa); literally "paradoxes," but in this context referring to ideas that go against common opinion.</note> handed down in this little work. For I would wish the reader to be persuaded that, just as I have established paths of philosophizing different from the common crowd, so I cannot approve of the simplicity of certain people. These are the ones who hold and believe what they were taught as children, or what Aristotle prescribed for them, so sacredly that they think nothing should be admitted except what <term>"he himself said"</term> <note>original: "αὐτὸς ἔφα" (autos epha); a Greek phrase equivalent to the Latin "ipse dixit," used to describe an uncritical appeal to authority—specifically Aristotle's.</note>. 

Indeed, I have frequently wondered why some among the <term>Orthodox</term> <note>Meaning those who hold the correct religious faith, in this case, Catholic scholars.</note> have more faith in a <term>Pagan Philosopher</term> than in either Holy Scripture or the decrees of the <term>Holy Fathers</term> <note>original: "SS. PP." (Sanctorum Patrum); the influential early Christian theologians.</note> who interpret it. The whole study of that philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> was placed in this, and all the weight and strength of his arguments concerning celestial philosophy seem to have aimed at building up his opinion on the <term>eternity of the world</term>—a view so contrary to Christian Doctrine. 

Therefore, having left behind these opinions unworthy of a Christian Philosopher, I have examined principles concerning the philosophy of the world with long and persistent study. I have done so according to the exact rule of the <term>combinatorial</term> <note>A method of logic, often associated with Ramon Llull and later Athanasius Kircher, that uses the systematic combination of concepts to discover universal truths.</note> and <term>analogical arts</term>. From the wonderful connection of all things, and the necessary dependence of all things upon individuals and individuals upon all things, I have deduced some <term>conclusions</term> <note>original: "confectaria"; logical deductions or corollaries.</note> which, although to some pe-

<summary>In this concluding section, the author defends his unconventional cosmological theories by criticizing those who prioritize Aristotle’s pagan philosophy over Holy Scripture. He introduces his methodology based on the "combinatorial" and "analogical" arts to explain the interconnectedness of the universe.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Holy Scripture, Church Fathers, pagan philosophy, combinatorial art, analogy, eternity of the world, cosmology</keywords>
